+# S04 — Defect-latched metallization for buried interconnect opens
+
+15 October 2026, Australia/Brisbane. **Status: untested construction; consequential manufacturing advantage NOT_ACHIEVED; novelty UNKNOWN.** This is an original proposed *combination and test contract*, not a report of fabrication. The mathematical voltage-collapse obstruction below is derived here under its stated circuit model. Literature results are attributed to their authors. No laboratory experiment was available.
+
+## Exact manufacturing task and why local information exists
+
+Target a narrow class: isolated open gaps (initially 4–100 nm, to be measured, not assumed repairable) in Cu micro-joints or low-current interconnect test structures inside an otherwise sealed 3D package. The endpoint is a *durable electrical connection between the two intended terminals* under specified current, temperature, and cycling, while adjacent intended-isolated nets remain isolated. It is not restoration of the original grain structure, a general cure for buried porosity, or repair of arbitrary shorts, delamination, wrong routes, missing pads, or blocked ion paths.
+
+The proposed substrate writes the binary target locally. Each vulnerable joint has two intended mating Cu electrodes surrounded by its own ion-conducting repair sleeve, Cu reservoir, and insulating barrier to every other net. The sleeve and electrode geometry say *which two ends may connect*. A temporary wafer-sort bus applies a bounded test bias to each known net; it need not image or locate the bad joint. A sound joint almost shorts the two ends, whereas an open places a large fraction of the test voltage across its local gap. Cu oxidation, ion migration and reduction can then nucleate a bridge at that gap. That is a physical selection operation, with the netlist, material deposition and isolation sleeve carrying information acquired during original manufacture. The location is selected by the defect-induced potential distribution rather than external full-volume tomography.
+
+This is not a free information oracle. Per-joint lithography, paired-electrode alignment, initial sleeve continuity, per-net addressability, isolation, electrolyte chemistry, and a voltage/current recipe are all supplied. A gap outside a sleeve or a broken reservoir is inaccessible. Multiple opens on one net divide voltage; shorts can redirect it. A process that merely reconnects a wire with an atomic filament may fail the actual endpoint.
+
+## First construction and a sharp self-limitation
+
+The first construction is a Cu-ion-conducting jacket (an oxide/solid electrolyte or confined gel to be qualified) around each preselected joint, with one Cu source electrode, an opposing reduction surface, a dielectric wall between neighboring nets, and a series-compliant test pulse. An open triggers electrochemical metallization; when Cu first bridges, its resistance falls and the gap voltage collapses. The field acts as a local sensor, power source and stop signal. The central idea is **already demonstrated in a different substrate**: [Gao et al. 2026](https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202529989) report flexible Ag printed circuits with an isolation layer and colloidal electrolyte; damage draws electrolyte into a crack and normal operating voltage drives electrochemical migration to reconnect the trace. Their abstract reports approximately 100% current recovery in hours and up to 350,000 bending cycles for the metal trace; the detailed repaired-joint life data were not available in the inspected abstract. Separately, Cu/HfO2/Pt cells with a **4 nm** HfO2 layer show field-assisted Cu-rich filaments and abrupt conductance changes, with current compliance essential to control formation [Lv et al. 2015](https://www.nature.com/articles/srep13311). An in-situ Cu/Al2O3 study directly saw filament growth and a post-connection no-growth period [Hubbard et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.nanolett.5b00901). These experiments do **not** establish repair of 100 nm buried interconnect gaps, long-term current capacity, or a reliable Cu joint.
+
+Here is the decisive elementary circuit calculation. If a source `V0` drives an emerging bridge resistance `Rb` through a safety/series resistance `Rs`, then
+
+```text
+Vgap = V0 Rb/(Rs + Rb).
+```
+
+Assume, illustratively, growth requires `Vgap >= V*`. For `0 < V* < V0`, growth must stop as `Rb` falls below `Rstop = V* Rs/(V0-V*)`. A passive resistor chosen to cap bridge current at `Imax` must obey `Rs >= V0/Imax`, hence `Rstop >= V* V0/[Imax(V0-V*)]`. With **assumed**, not measured, `V0 = 1 V`, `V* = 0.2 V`, and `Imax = 100 microampere`, `Rs >= 10 kilohm` and `Rstop >= 2.5 kilohm`. A 100 nm-long, 100 nm × 100 nm Cu bridge would have only `~0.168 ohm` if bulk Cu resistivity `1.68e-8 ohm m` applied. Maintaining 0.2 V across it would require `~1.19 A`; the passive resistor needed to let growth continue to that resistance would be `<=0.672 ohm`, allowing `>=1.49 A` in the source model. This is a conflict between safe forming current and passive voltage-driven *thickening*. It is not a universal electrochemical impossibility; its assumptions must be measured and alternative mechanisms can bypass it.
+
+The bulk-resistivity cylinder equivalent at 2.5 kilohm and 100 nm length has radius only `~0.46 nm`. Bulk resistivity and continuum geometry are **not valid predictions at atomic scale**; the estimate merely shows that the stop resistance is in the atomic-filament regime, where contact resistance, quantized conductance and stochastic rupture matter. At 100 microampere, a hypothetical 0.5 nm-radius bridge would carry `~1.3e14 A/m^2`, versus `1e10 A/m^2` in a 100 nm × 100 nm cross-section. Neither figure establishes a safe current limit without accelerated-life data. In a measured particle-trapping circuit, electrical contact caused the local field to disappear and stopped further particle attraction; excessive post-bridge current destroyed the bridge through heating [Suetsugu and Iwase 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9967765/). The particular chemistry differs, but the endpoint tension is directly relevant.
+
+For a 100 nm × 100 nm × 100 nm Cu bridge, Faraday's law gives the *ideal stoichiometric* `Q = 2 F rho_Cu volume/M_Cu = 2.72e-11 C` (27 pC), or 27 pJ of electrical work at 1 V. This counts only Cu atoms: no ion transport inefficiency, reservoir preparation, electrode reactions, test overhead, heat, leakage, or substrate processing. At 1 nA of 100%-efficient Faradaic current it would take 27 ms, but actual geometry, kinetics and parasitic electronic current are unmeasured. There is no measured energy or time advantage here.
+
+## Substantive redesign: field-write a repair catalyst, then chemically thicken
+
+To address the skinny-filament obstruction, separate *selection* from *load-bearing growth*. The proposed redesign puts a finite Cu precursor/reductant supply in a sealed annular repair chamber around each joint. A high-gap-field step would create an active metal/catalyst seed only at an open, effectively latching the local defect decision. A subsequent electroless Cu reaction would thicken that seed after the electrical voltage has collapsed. Reagent volume would be bounded by the chamber; a passivating wall and the eventual closure of the gap would limit spread. A final low-energy electrical challenge would reject tenuous bridges before the package is accepted. In symbols, the hoped-for gate is `open -> high local field -> catalyst seed -> chemical growth -> thick connection`, while `intact -> low local field -> no seed`.
+
+This is a hypothesis with hard missing interfaces. Electrochemical catalyst writing must depend on the *gap field*, not merely the absolute potential of an intact Cu pad in the bath. Electroless chemistry must remain shelf-stable through bonding and thermal history, reach an actually buried crack, keep reaction products or gas from trapping voids, and stop before Cu shorts neighboring nets. If cracks themselves expose Cu catalyst, a purely chemical incumbent may start plating without the field-write stage; the additional electrical stage then supplies no advantage. If the reaction continues on all intact exposed Cu, local selectivity is lost. No published source inspected here demonstrates all these gates simultaneously in a sealed, dense 3D package.
+
+The nearest primary evidence cuts both ways. A 2024 chip-to-chip study used microfluidically delivered electroless Cu to join aligned Cu bumps and directly observed voids at gaps as low as **10 micrometres**, attributed to trapped hydrogen and uneven reagent flow. Intermittent flow and inhibitor changes reduced voids, but the paper also describes extraneous Cu on Si [Ren et al. 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11123229/). This establishes relevant deposition and concrete transport/side-reaction hazards, not our sealed-chamber repair. An earlier microcapsule experiment restored nearly full circuit conductance in under 1 ms after a crack released liquid Ga–In [Blaiszik et al. 2012](https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.201102888); it demonstrates local fracture-triggered reagent access but at a much larger device scale and with a liquid-metal endpoint. A paper on area-selective Ni electrodeposition reports full tensile-strength recovery in selected fractured metal samples, including a 3D-printed shellular structure [Akbari et al. 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36933269/), but those electrolyte-accessible fractures do not establish dense, sealed Cu interconnect repair.
+
+## Strongest equally informed manufacturing comparator
+
+For the proposed chip-to-chip joint manufacturing stage, the strongest direct comparator is **optimized electroless all-Cu interconnection**, using the *same* pad layout, alignment tolerances, precursor access, microfluidic or chamber infrastructure, test contacts, thermal budget and acceptance criteria. The [2024 primary study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11123229/) shows the method and its voiding mechanisms. Give it the same geometry and reagent budget; it may connect weak joints without field-written catalyst, eliminate per-net repair pulses, and exploit improved flow/inhibitors. If the setting is post-seal or flexible circuit repair, [Gao et al.'s operational-voltage-driven electrochemical repair](https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.202529989) is the closest mechanism comparator; it must get the same addressability and repair-medium access. A further benchmark is preinstalled repair channels plus electroless chemistry triggered by a fracture-exposed surface; the proposed sleeve and reagent cannot be charged only to the competitor. For low-current lines, [field-assisted particle bridging](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-019-55801-8) and [electrochemical metallization](https://www.nature.com/articles/srep13311) are also known active local selectors. Plain field-directed reconnection has no plausible priority claim.
+
+Thus the candidate only earns attention if field-writing a durable catalytic latch improves *total* good-joint yield, low-ohm fatigue survival, and adjacent-net isolation at equal manufacturing and test cost. Merely avoiding site-by-site imaging is not a unique advantage: pad geometry, bath exposure, continuity testing, and self-aligned electroless growth already exploit local information. Conventional electrical redundancy/rerouting during package test is another equally informed functional comparator when physical Cu restoration is not needed; its masks, spare wires and test time would have to be counted rather than dismissed.
+
+## Selectivity, endpoint and scaling contract
+
+Let `M` be intact repair-capable joints, `D` be open joints, `p_false` the per-intact-joint probability of a new short or damaging deposition, and `p_repair` the per-open probability of a connection meeting the *aged* endpoint. If failures were independent, a necessary system-yield condition is `(1-p_false)^M p_repair^D >= Y`. Even ignoring open-repair failures, for `M = 10^6` and `Y = 0.9` we require `p_false <= 1 - 0.9^(1/10^6) = 1.0536e-7`. Even ignoring false deposition, for `D = 10` we require `p_repair >= 0.9^(1/10) = 0.98952`. Correlations and common-mode chemistry can make the independence formula optimistic. With zero false events, about `2.84e7` representative intact-joint trials would be needed merely to put a one-sided 95% binomial upper bound below `1.0536e-7`; a small coupon study cannot certify million-joint yield. These numbers are original arithmetic on a hypothetical yield contract, not measured rates. The circuit, charge and yield arithmetic is reproduced by [`verify_circuit.py`](./verify_circuit.py).
+
+Endpoint verification must be staged. During wafer sort, per-net four-terminal resistance and neighboring-net leakage can establish functional connectivity and isolation for the addressed nets. Stress at the specified current, thermal cycles, repeated pulse/read cycles and noise/drift measurements probe whether the connection persists. Destructive cross-sections or X-ray/TEM sampling on blinded coupons must check whether growth made a dense joined cross-section or a filament plus hidden void. Terminal resistance alone cannot distinguish two internal states with identical `R` but very different neck geometry, electromigration hazard or crack resistance. The production endpoint must state allowable `R`, leakage, drift, current density, temperature and lifetime *before* looking at results.
+
+Full resource accounting includes: extra mask/alignment steps to make each sleeve and reservoir; lost area and added capacitance; Cu contamination barriers; ionic/chemical stability during all subsequent heat steps; precursor and reductant manufacture, loading and waste; test-bus routing and per-net pulse energy/time; bad-gap localization implicitly performed by the field; any chemical bath/transport and gas removal; rejected dies; accelerated testing; and reliability under operation. A bridge formed in an unqualified sleeve does not waive these costs. The physical target is stored in lithographic geometry and therefore pays a preparation cost up front.
+
+## Decisive next test and disposition
+
+Fabricate blinded arrays of intentionally intact, intentionally open, partially resistive and adjacent-short Cu joint coupons in the *same* package-relevant stack, with calibrated gap distributions and independent measurement of sleeve/reagent access. Randomize coupon assignment to: (A) proposed field-write plus chemical growth, (B) the strongest tuned electroless-only process with the same channels/reagents, (C) field-write/filament alone, and (D) untreated control. Record all applied voltages, currents, charge and time. Dissect selected joints after stress to measure metal thickness, trapped voids, contamination and shorts. A first gate is that A materially beats B on aged low-resistance yield and isolation at matched total cost; if it only produces fast high-resistance filaments, or B matches it, stop this line. Scale to representative package arrays only after the coupon gate; the intact-joint false-action bound above is a separate large-sample qualification problem.
+
+**Disposition:** the local-field idea is physically motivated but old in its basic form. The two-stage latch-and-thicken construction addresses a real mathematical obstruction, but its key selectivity, access, stable chemical storage and endpoint claims are untested, and an equally informed electroless process may absorb the same benefit. This is a falsifiable manufacturing research proposal, **not** a demonstrated new capability.
+

+# Adversarial audit of the opposite-order NV pulse contrast
+
+15 October 2026. This audits [`s09_joint_quantum/REPORT.md`](../s09_joint_quantum/REPORT.md) without altering it. **Verdict:** the amplitude contrast is a valid way to reject responses linear in commanded pulse amplitude under matched initial states. It is a generic nonlinear, history-dependent response statistic. A nonzero (K_r) does not identify Fe/Li2O contact blocking, an interfacial failure precursor, or a site-specific current partition. Existing bipolar-pulse nonlinear characterization and nonlinear electrochemical spectroscopy already claim the broader measurement class; embedded NVs supply genuinely local magnetic access, but ordinary operando NV readout with the *same four pulse arms* contains every datum needed to compute (K_r). A consequential decision beyond those incumbents is unproven. The most useful rescue is a narrowly defined, validated local *waveform susceptibility* assay, with a same-site crossover gate and an independent chemical/thermal test.
+
+## What the algebra actually isolates
+
+Let the two order means at pulse magnitude (U) produce (C(U)=\mathbb E[y_{+-}(U)-y_{-+}(U)]), and form (K_r=C(rU)-rC(U)). If the waveform shape and initial-state distribution are identical and the entire input-to-field map is linear, (C(rU)=rC(U)). That cancellation is correct, even for an unknown linear memory kernel. For a smooth polarity-symmetric protocol, however,
+
+\[
+C(U)=c_1U+c_3U^3+c_5U^5+\cdots,
+\qquad K_r=(r^3-r)c_3U^3+(r^5-r)c_5U^5+\cdots.
+\]
+
+Thus two amplitudes remove a first-order term but do not isolate a unique third-order chemical mechanism, and at finite amplitudes do not isolate the cubic coefficient. The short-time Lie bracket in S09 is mathematically valid for its assumed dynamics, yet all smooth dissipative stateful mechanisms have vector fields and potentially nonzero brackets. The bracket is not a fingerprint for a hidden contact state. This is directly related to nonlinear electrochemical impedance and bipolar-pulse analysis, which have demonstrated charge-transfer, diffusion, OCV, hysteresis and amplifier contributions to nonlinear responses [Murbach et al. 2018; Kirk et al. 2023; Ernst et al. 2019; Li et al. 2024]. The (+/-) order and amplitude contrast may be a convenient *time-domain projection* of these effects, but not a new source of information compared with the complete pulse and NV time series.
+
+## Exact same-output thermal countermodel
+
+S09's toy model has a hidden even-in-current contact state (z): (\dot x=vu(1-z)), (\dot z=a u^2-bz), (y=kx). Starting from (z=0), its endpoint result is (K_r=2kva(r^3-r)U^3(1-e^{-b\tau})^2/b^2). The following **different physical model produces the identical formula, including the pulse-duration dependence and a persistent local-charge difference after the pulses**:
+
+\[
+\dot\theta=a_Tu^2-b\theta,\qquad
+\dot x=vu(1-\beta\theta),\qquad y=kx.
+\]
+
+Here (\theta) is local temperature above baseline, (a_Tu^2) is Joule heat divided by heat capacity, (b^{-1}) is a cooling time, and temperature changes the fraction of total current entering the magnetic Fe-associated pathway relative to a parallel carbon/SEI/other pathway. Such a temperature dependence can arise from different kinetic activation energies; no contact blocking or damage state is postulated. The two orders have exactly the same ​\(u^2(t)\), so they share a rising temperature trajectory. They apply opposite current signs in opposite thermal order. Substitution gives
+
+\[
+C_T(U,\tau)=\frac{2kv\beta a_TU^3}{b^2}(1-e^{-b\tau})^2,
+\quad K_{r,T}=(r^3-r)C_T(U,\tau).
+\]
+
+Choosing \(\beta a_T=a\) makes *all four post-pulse NV field means' order/amplitude contrast* match S09's toy result for every (U, r, \tau) in the model. Because \(\dot x=0\) at zero current, extending the zero-current NV-read delay does not distinguish these two models. A nonmagnetic-electrode sham also fails: the thermal alternative depends on Fe-associated magnetic current partition and vanishes without Fe. An optical-only heating sham at zero current fails for the same reason; the false positive needs the heat–current interaction. This is a structural identifiability obstruction for the proposed readout, not evidence that thermal coupling has the required magnitude in the proposed specimen.
+
+The thermal alternative is physically serious in this exact apparatus. The embedded-NV primary study says focused laser light heated some electrode locations, uses the NV zero-field splitting as a temperature indicator, and notes that current generates Joule heat [Liu et al. 2024]. The paper's carbon/Fe3O4/PVDF electrode has heterogeneous local conductive paths, and its different NV positions sampled markedly different surroundings. The Fe3O4/Li bulk-magnetometry study used a 3 T field specifically to suppress low-field anisotropy/interparticle-coupling ambiguity in its Fe-particle magnetic interpretation [Li et al. 2021]; Liu's local NV readout used about 89 G. This does not prove a low-field artifact, but it means a fixed-bias local stray-field change cannot be assumed proportional to a unique Fe surface-charge change. Measuring the NV's own temperature helps but does not certify the temperature of each reactive Fe/electrolyte contact around it.
+
+## A thermal-independent nonlinear incumbent can also make cubic (K_r)
+
+Even an isothermal experiment can produce the same leading response through routine nonlinear current partition. Consider two reversible parallel local paths with common overpotential \(\eta\):
+
+\[
+j_F=g_F\eta+h_F\eta^3+O(\eta^5),\quad
+j_P=g_P\eta+h_P\eta^3+O(\eta^5),\quad u=j_F+j_P.
+\]
+
+An odd cubic term is ordinary for a symmetric Butler–Volmer expansion; asymmetric kinetics and concentration dependence create further terms. Invert the total-current relation with (G=g_F+g_P). Then
+
+\[
+j_F=\frac{g_F}{G}u+
+\frac{h_Fg_P-g_Fh_P}{G^4}u^3+O(u^5)
+  =c_1u+c_3u^3+O(u^5).
+\]
+
+If a local reversible magnetic/ionic state relaxes as \(\dot q=-bq+j_F\) and NV output is (y=kq), exact two-pulse integration to cubic order gives
+
+\[
+C(U,\tau)=-\frac{2k(c_1U+c_3U^3)}{b}(1-e^{-b\tau})^2+O(U^5),
+\quad K_r=-\frac{2kc_3(r^3-r)U^3}{b}(1-e^{-b\tau})^2+O(U^5).
+\]
+
+This matches S09's cubic amplitude and pulse-duration signature by choosing the physically unconstrained path coefficients. It requires no even-in-current gate (z). A long rest would attenuate this specific (q) model, unlike the thermal model above, but finite-delay measurements alone can be matched, and persistence cannot rule out the thermal model. The calculation is an analytic counterexample, not a fitted specimen or a claim that these path coefficients occur in Fe3O4. The primary NLEIS literature explicitly observes and models nonlinear charge transfer, OCV and diffusion, and the 2024 bipolar-pulsing study measures nonlinear voltage/hysteresis from thousands of pulses in commercial cells; these are credible incumbents for the *type* of signal.
+
+## The proposed location map is not identified by sacrificial lanes
+
+S09 proposes four randomized arms on separate, matched microelectrode lanes because exact resetting of a potentially damaged Fe/Li2O site is not guaranteed. This identifies \(\mathbb E[Y_s]\) for each arm (s\) over a population of lanes, assuming randomization and no interference. It does **not** identify the individual potential-outcome difference (Y_j(+,-)-Y_j(-,+)) for the same buried Fe/NV/contact network (j). Its headline “map of locations where order changes the local magnetic state” is therefore too strong unless each exact location can be measured in a verified reversible within-site crossover. Nominally corresponding image coordinates on two fabricated lanes are different microstructures and different NV-to-Fe distances. Liu et al. observed that some NV diamonds were likely near active material and others near binder/carbon, so this is not a merely statistical nicety.
+
+The proposed lanes also share an optical/thermal environment and, as phrased, one Li half-cell. If they share electrolyte/counter-electrode, a pulse in one lane can alter neighboring ionic concentration, potential and heat; electrical addressability does not guarantee independent potential outcomes. The experiment needs either separately sealed microcells or a measured cross-talk bound with one lane pulsed and the others electrically idle. Otherwise random assignment of four arms within one common electrolyte is not an independent randomized trial. A site-specific claim and a population-average claim should be kept distinct throughout.
+
+## Equal-budget competitors and decision value
+
+The strongest same-information competitor is **the identical embedded-NV apparatus, four pulse arms, all raw ODMR spectra, current/voltage/temperature histories, and the same samples and measurement time**, analyzed as an ordinary operando NV transient with a flexible nonlinear response model. It can calculate (K_r) from those raw means exactly. If (D) denotes all acquired data and (K_r=f(D)), then the best decision based on (D) has no worse achievable expected loss than the best decision based on (K_r). The extra computation is negligible beside optical acquisition and cell fabrication but must be recorded. Thus (K_r) may be a robust predeclared statistic or simplification, yet it cannot give information inaccessible to the equal-access NV incumbent.
+
+A lower-cost competitor uses the same four bipolar current arms, terminal voltage/current/temperature and, where feasible, electrode-resolved voltage, analyzed by established pulse/NLEIS methods. Ernst et al. already used opposite-polarity current pulses of increasing magnitude to measure current–overpotential nonlinearity, and Li et al. characterized nonlinear OCV/hysteresis with bipolar pulses. This electrical competitor will miss genuinely local *magnetic* Fe behavior; the point of embedded NV must be a decision that requires that spatial magnetic variable, not generic detection of nonlinearity. A fair trial should allow the electrical competitor an equal specimen/energy/time budget, and allow the equal-access NV comparator its exact data. Standard low-amplitude linear EIS or a no-sensor CCCV policy is too weak.
+
+The only immediately supported scientific output of a positive (K_r) is: “at this calibrated magnetic site or site population, the two charge-balanced pulse orders give a field response whose amplitude scaling is not linear.” It says nothing by itself about Fe oxidation state, irreversible damage, contact blockage, preferred future waveform, or extra recoverable capacity. One *potentially* useful downstream decision is to choose which pulse order minimizes subsequent site-level Fe conversion mismatch or fade, but that predictive relation has to be shown prospectively. If the thermal twin predicts the same outcome, it is still a possible empirical predictor but no unique new mechanism; if an equal-data NV model performs as well, there is no independent operational advantage.
+
+## Narrow rescue and decisive test
+
+First establish pulse-level reversible resetting in the exact formed Fe/Li2O voltage window. Bulk Li et al. report highly reversible capacitive-like magnetization there, which makes this plausible, but their result does not prove exact reset for an embedded NV site's local structure or heat. On *one registered NV/Fe site*, alternate all four arms in randomized crossover order, separated by an independently checked return of full ODMR spectrum, electrode potential, temperature and local chemical proxy to baseline. If crossover cannot be validated, report only population-average (K_r), not a site map. Use independent electrolyte compartments or bound cross-lane interference experimentally. Record actual current integrals, voltage, cell energy, optical/microwave dose, full multi-orientation ODMR spectra and elapsed scan time; this source demonstrated minute-scale site tracking, not the required pulse-resolution floor.
+
+The mechanism-discriminating intervention is a **thermal factorial on the Fe cell itself**. At fixed electrochemical pulses, alter heat removal or apply calibrated external heating so that the local thermal trajectory is measured and changed; repeat under an isothermal clamp if feasible. Require a joint fit to Fe-site NV thermometry plus a contact-proximate independent thermometer, with uncertainty for the temperature difference between sensor and reactive interface. A nonmagnetic sham or optical-only sham is insufficient. Vary magnetic bias within the calibrated NV range and corroborate the Fe phase/valence/charge state independently on matched sacrificial sites; this checks low-field magnetization/geometry explanations. Test multiple amplitudes and pulse lengths so a cubic small-signal region and higher-order terms can be separated. Any claimed chemical assignment needs the independent chemical result, not a field fit alone.
+
+Finally preregister a *held-out decision*: from a low-dose (K_r) assay, predict either which of two subsequently applied waveform orders reduces site-specific irreversible Fe/Li2O change or which sites will exhibit excess fade after a fixed stress protocol. Compare blinded predictions and full acquisition-inclusive costs with (i) the same-data NV transient/model competitor and (ii) the equal-budget electrical bipolar/NLEIS competitor. If same-site crossover fails, thermal/low-field confounds fully explain (K_r), or (K_r) adds no held-out decision value over the same-data NV model, the proposed operation is a useful contrast at most. If all gates pass, the result would establish a task-specific local susceptibility/prediction protocol. It still would not establish a quantum advantage or priority for the general nonlinear pulse method.
+
+## Primary evidence actually inspected
+
+* [Liu et al., *Operando quantum sensing captures the nanoscale electrochemical evolution in batteries*, Device 2, 100521 (2024)](https://www.iop.cas.cn/xwzx/kydt/202409/P020240924528848148977.pdf): inspected experimental procedures, pages 3–7. +# Storage intervention: constant-throughput local current transfer in a segmented graphite cell
+
+**Status (15 October 2026): conditional design and falsifiable test; no laboratory result; novelty not established.** The generic architecture is substantially anticipated. The narrower useful hypothesis is that deliberately transferring charge current from a locally plating-prone region to a healthier region, while keeping total charge current fixed, can delay plating in a large pouch cell. The transfer is valuable only if the cell has a controllable spatial differential mode and the healthier region has spare anode *and cathode* margin. A control experiment must measure those facts; cell-level voltage or a fitted impedance alone cannot establish them.
+
+## Physical problem and chosen operation
+
+During fast charging of graphite cells, local intercalation kinetics, electrolyte transport, temperature, state of lithiation, and current-collector geometry differ across the electrode. Lithium metal may deposit in one location before the aggregate voltage, current, or temperature signals become distinctive. Direct imaging has found plating preferentially on fast-lithiating particles and redistribution of plated lithium during rest [Chen et al., 2021]. In a segmented LFP/graphite pouch cell, measured current across ten positive-electrode segments was nonuniform and changed pattern during discharge [Zhang et al., 2013]. Neither measurement licenses a particular fast-charge controller, but both defeat the assumption that one terminal current describes every local electrochemical load.
+
+Build a *laboratory* two-to-four-zone graphite/NMC pouch cell with electronically isolated anode current-collector/coating islands, independent bidirectional current channels, individual current shunts, and spatially registered reference-electrode contacts. Keep the separator and cathode chemistry otherwise matched to an ordinary pouch. An isolated anode coating is essential: merely cutting the copper while leaving a continuous conductive coating could bridge the islands. The electronics deliver a total charge current (I=\sum_i I_i), but can change the vector (I_i). While charging, apply a short compensated transfer, (I_1\mapsto I_1-\delta), (I_2\mapsto I_2+\delta). This preserves immediate total charge delivery. Record each region's potential relative to its local reference, current, and temperature before and after the transfer. If the vulnerable region's calibrated plating margin rises and the receiving region remains within its own anode/cathode limits, retain the new split. If not, lower total current. The useful operation is **current transfer conditional on demonstrated spatial control authority**, not a renamed impedance classifier.
+
+The primary physical target is the local Li deposition reaction overpotential at the graphite/electrolyte interface, not the pack voltage. Xiong et al. experimentally separated plating reaction overpotential from graphite surface equilibrium potential and reported plating when the former became negative; they explicitly cautioned that the common graphite-vs-Li potential criterion is incomplete [Xiong et al., 2023]. An embedded reference reads an electrode/electrolyte potential at its finite location, not the minimum interfacial overpotential over all pores and particles. Thus a controller can use a *calibrated conservative lower bound* on plating margin, not pretend that a reference-electrode number directly certifies every microscopic site. A cathode local-potential and temperature bound must be checked too: sending current to the apparently healthy anode region can overdelithiate or heat the corresponding positive electrode.
+
+## Original conditional mechanism
+
+The following is a local mathematical model and derivation, **not** a measured battery law. At a fixed cell state and over a short control interval, let (m_i>0) denote a conservative lower bound on the no-plating margin in zone (i), after accounting for sensor error and unresolved through-plane polarization. Linearize its dependence on the zone current vector:
+
+\[
+m(I+u)\simeq m(I)-A u,\qquad A_{ij}:=-\frac{\partial m_i}{\partial I_j}.
+\]
+
+The matrix (A) is a physical response matrix, not assumed diagonal or time invariant. Electrolyte coupling, common cathode potential, in-plane conduction, heat and adjacent particle states can create large off-diagonal terms. A brief current transfer probes a column difference while still delivering useful charge. For two zones, take (u=(-\delta,+\delta)), so (u_1+u_2=0). Then
+
+\[
+\Delta m_1\simeq \delta(A_{11}-A_{12}),\qquad
+\Delta m_2\simeq-\delta(A_{22}-A_{21}).
+\]
+
+If zone 1 needs a margin increase (d_1>0), zone 2 has spare margin (s_2>0), and both differential coefficients are positive, a constant-throughput correction exists in this linear interval precisely when
+
+\[
+\frac{d_1}{A_{11}-A_{12}}\leq\delta\leq
+\frac{s_2}{A_{22}-A_{21}},
+\]
+
+also subject to current limits, a cathode margin, temperature, and the finite validity interval of the linearization. If the left endpoint exceeds the right one, no current transfer satisfies both local margins; reduce total current or stop. If (A_{11}=A_{12}), moving current from zone 1 to 2 has no first-order protective effect on zone 1. This exposes a decisive **controllability** gate, distinct from whether a voltage trace contains a detectable feature. With (n) zones, the same gate is whether the measured/validated response (A) has an effective component on the zero-sum subspace \(\{u: \mathbf 1^Tu=0\}\) large enough, at actual noise and safety margins, to improve a constrained charge objective.
+
+An illustrative *dimensionless calculation* makes the conditional gain explicit. Suppose an invented two-zone margin law is (m=\mathbf 1-AI) with
+
+\[
+A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.1\\0.1&0.5\end{pmatrix},\qquad I_i\geq0.
+\]
+
+An equal-current bus (I_1=I_2=t) must use (t\leq1/1.1=0.9091), total current at most (1.8182). Independent currents can meet both active constraints at (I_1=0.8163, I_2=1.8367), total (2.6531), a 45.9% increase *in this fabricated model only*. If instead (A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}), every margin depends only on total current and segmentation gives **zero** charging advantage. Real values, uncertainty, drift, and boundary reactions decide which regime a cell occupies; the numerical example is not a performance prediction.
+
+There is also a limited information gain. One aggregate terminal voltage and current cannot uniquely report (n) local currents or local interfacial states: distinct spatial current/temperature/plating configurations can produce the same scalar sum. Segmented shunts directly report (I_i), and distributed reference contacts report spatially sampled electrode potentials. Compensated transfers reveal whether a local response is causally steerable at unchanged total current. They do *not* uniquely identify all pore-scale lithium metal, SEI, transport, or temperature states. The response can drift as SOC and temperature change. Crucially, turning a zone's external branch off may not extinguish internal ionic currents or pre-existing plated lithium; tomography has measured such currents during open-circuit rest after fast charge [ACS Nano study, 2023]. The operation aims to prevent new plating during charge, not guarantee that existing metal disappears or thermal runaway is impossible.
+
+## Closest work and the same-information comparator
+
+This is a crowded architecture. Zhang et al. (2013) built a ten-segment pouch with a continuous graphite negative electrode, segmented LFP positive electrode, individual 2 mΩ shunts, one bus, and one-second local current readings. Their device measured nonuniform current but did not independently control charging zones. The distinction matters: it gives experimental precedent for local acquisition, not a demonstration of the proposed intervention. US9343781B2 explicitly describes local collector pads, individual transistors, current/temperature sensors, and coordinated reduction of problematic-region current while increasing healthy-region current. This directly anticipates the general control architecture. Wang et al. (2025) report distributed reference contacts resolving local negative-electrode potential and using it to set fast-charge current boundaries. These are primary reasons to mark **architectural novelty as doubtful and specific protocol novelty UNKNOWN**, pending a proper patent/literature search. No advantage over the patent's implementation has been shown.
+
+The first matched comparator is a conventional single-current pouch using **the same distributed reference contacts, sampling, calibration, temperature measurements, and controller computation**. It follows the most restrictive measured zone and globally derates to keep all margins positive. Since its feasible controls are (I_i=w_i I), a subset of the ideal segmented controls, the segmented optimizer cannot be worse in the *ideal model* before hardware costs. This is a mathematical feasible-set fact, not an empirical advantage. The second and stronger systems comparator is a bank of smaller, sealed cells occupying the same gross volume, each with its own measurements and charge channel. It has the same spatial information and at least as much independent electrical control, with less cross-zone ionic coupling, but more casing, tabs, and pack assembly. A segmented pouch is consequential only if its retained active-material fraction, mass, heat handling, wiring reliability, and cost beat this modular incumbent at equal delivered energy, lifetime and plating risk. Existing potential-controlled fast charging and distributed-reference protocols already provide a serious global-current baseline; comparing against simple CCCV would be too weak [Rangarajan et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2025].
+
+## Acquisition, physical costs, and failure channels
+
+* **Preparation:** patterned/insulated collector and graphite coating, edge sealing and pouch feedthroughs, calibrated distributed references, per-zone shunts and current channels. Trenches may create edge current crowding or consume capacity. Segmentation demonstrated for measurement does not establish manufacturable, durable, independently driven large-format cells.
+* **Acquisition:** every pulse consumes time and charge redistribution, plus reference calibration and a plating ground truth. A reference sample can miss through-plane minima or drift. The physical claim requires uncertainty bounds from paired operando/post-mortem studies, not fitting a voltage threshold on the same traces later used to claim success.
+* **Energy and control:** switches and shunts dissipate approximately \(\int\sum_i I_i^2 R_i\,dt\), before multi-channel conversion, sensing and cooling energy. A linear-pass transistor additionally wastes \(\int\sum_i I_i V_{\rm drop,i}\,dt\); a switched converter could lower that at the cost of size and complexity. Moving current to a healthy region can increase its heat and cathode stress. Total charger power and bus voltage constraints still apply.
+* **Reliability:** a stuck-on channel, short between coating islands, failed reference, broken seal, or fast state drift can invalidate local control. A fail-safe design reverts to globally conservative derating, but the failure probability and diagnostic coverage must be measured. Region isolation must be verified electrically and under electrolyte soak, swelling, aging and abuse.
+* **Scaling:** channel count, wiring, reference leads, feedthrough sealing, and controller power grow with zone number. Too few zones cannot isolate a small hot spot; too many shrink net capacity and raise failure opportunities. The optimum zone scale is an experimental question.
+
+## Decisive experiment
+
+Make randomized matched graphite/NMC pouch prototypes from the same lot: (A) ordinary single-current geometry with distributed reference contacts and the strongest validated global-margin controller; (B) independently driven two/four-zone geometry with the same contacts and controller budget; (C) same gross-volume modular small-cell bank with per-cell control. Include an ordinary segmented prototype with its channels hard-bussed to quantify manufacturing penalties separately from control benefit. Introduce one reproducible local handicap, such as a controlled colder region or a measured transport variation, while keeping global thermal conditions and initial SOC matched. First make small compensated current transfers at sub-plating rates. Estimate (A_{11}-A_{12}), (A_{22}-A_{21}), repeatability and uncertainty while recording both electrode potentials and temperature. If the differential authority is absent or reverses under SOC/temperature variation, the mechanism fails before risky cycling.
+
+Then compare preregistered **charge-time versus plating-risk Pareto curves** at equal delivered usable energy, with the same maximum cell temperature, voltage, cathode margin, charger power, and energy overhead accounted for. Quantify local metallic Li immediately after selected charges using a validated destructive local assay, with microscopy/cross-section or operando spectroscopic confirmation and sham controls; track irreversible Li loss and capacity fade over repeated cycles. Do not infer zero plating from absence of a voltage feature. Randomize cell assignment; report failed sensors, dead channels, region-to-region variance, false-negative local margins, reference drift and the cost of all pulses and sensing. A successful result requires (i) measured differential response of the predicted sign and sufficient size, (ii) less local plated Li at equal total charge/time or faster charge at equal measured plating/cathode/thermal risk, **and** (iii) net system benefit against the modular comparator. If (i) or (ii) fails, the physical intervention is refuted for that cell family. If (iii) fails, it remains a useful laboratory diagnostic/control demonstration but not a consequential storage capability.
+
+## Primary sources actually inspected
+
+1. [Zhang, Shaffer, Wang and Rahn, *In-Situ Measurement of Current Distribution in a Li-Ion Cell*, J. Electrochem. Soc. 160 A610 (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1149/2.046304jes). The [author-hosted full PDF](https://ecec.me.psu.edu/Pubs/046304JES.pdf) was downloaded and text-extracted into `sources/`. Inspected the abstract, full experimental cell and shunt setup, and results. It reports ten segmented positive electrodes in a graphite/LFP pouch, a continuous negative electrode, parallel bus through 2 mΩ shunts, and evolving nonuniform local currents. It does **not** test independent charge-current control or local plating prevention.
+2. [US9343781B2, *Adaptive current-collector electrochemical system*](https://patents.google.com/patent/US9343781B2). Inspected detailed description and claims: region collector pads, individual transistors, local current/temperature sensors, and coordinated region current control. This is explicit prior art for the architectural core; this report makes no priority claim.
+3. [Wang et al., *Distributed reference electrode for lithium plating detection and fast charging optimization in Lithium-Ion batteries*, Chemical Engineering Journal 513, 162990 (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cej.2025.162990). Inspected publisher highlights/abstract: spatial negative-electrode potential monitoring and fast-charge boundary calibration. Full methods were not accessible in this pass; detailed resolution and reliability are not independently verified here.
+4. [Xiong et al., *Revealing the onset condition of Li plating on graphite electrodes under fast-charging*, J. Mater. Chem. A 11, 16605 (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1039/D3TA02968A). Inspected publisher abstract: reports negative Li plating reaction overpotential as the onset condition in their decoupling experiments, not simply graphite terminal potential. Full derivation was not inspected.
+5. [Chen et al., *Operando video microscopy of Li plating and re-intercalation on graphite anodes during fast charging*, J. Mater. Chem. A 9, 23522 (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1039/D1TA06023F). Inspected publisher abstract: local fast-lithiating particles plate first, and plating/reintercalation signatures occur during rest/discharge. Cell format and measured images were not reanalysed here.
+6. [*Large Local Currents in a Lithium-Ion Battery during Rest after Fast Charging*, ACS Nano 17, 19180 (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.3c05470). Inspected PubMed abstract: operando X-ray microtomography inferred internal currents after 6C charge while external current was zero, including spatial outliers. This supports the limitation on post-charge protection, not a control result.
+7. [Rangarajan, Barsukov and Mukherjee, *Anode potential controlled charging prevents lithium plating*, J. Mater. Chem. A (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1039/D0TA04467A). Inspected publisher abstract: direct anode-potential-controlled charging and improved cycle life under tested conditions. It is a strong whole-cell control comparator, not evidence that segmentation helps.
+
+**Provenance:** equations, controllability condition, dimensionless example, and experimental design are original analysis in this report. The cell architecture is prior art. +much progress has been made, grand challenges remain. 3–6 In partic-
+ular, how to unlock the potential of existing Li battery materials and
+to scale up Li-ion cells to 10-100 Ah sizes without substantial loss
+in performance, durability and safety remains a key technological
+challenge.
+Large Li-ion batteries are critical for vehicle and grid energy stor-
+age that would enable a sustainable energy future. In large-format Li-
+ion batteries, especially cylindrical and prismatic ones in which elec-
+trodes, separators and current collectors are wound or multi-layered,
+the pathways of current (e.g. through foil current collectors) and heat
+(e.g. through multi-layer rolls from inside to outside) are typically
+not equal at different locations of electrodes. Through complex in-
+teractions among the local reaction current, state of charge (SOC)
+and temperature, non-uniform spatial distribution of these critical pa-
+rameters is inevitable, especially during high C-rate operation. These
+non-uniform distributions will lead to under-utilization of active ma-
+terials loaded in a large cell, thereby drastically reducing its energy
+density from the coin cell benchmark. Indeed, the modeling study of
+Zhao et al. 7 revealed, for the ﬁrst time, a direct and signiﬁcant corre-
+lation between cell energy density and the non-uniformity in current
+distribution, as well as a potential to gain as much as 45% in cell energy
+density through improving the current distribution in a large Li-ion
+cell. Of equal importance, non-uniform current distribution results in
+localized overcharge or overdischarge, compromising durability and
+safety of large batteries. Therefore, understanding how these critical
+parameters distribute under various design and operation conditions
+greatly aids development of energy denser, safer, and more durable
+Li-ion batteries.
+In recent years, electrochemical modeling has been widely used in
+the research and development of Li-ion batteries to gain insight into
+internal processes, predict performance, optimize cell design and op-
+eration, and accelerate development of new concepts/strategies.8–15 A
+critical element for exercising battery models is experimental valida-
+tion. Due to the non-uniform distribution of those critical parameters
+∗ Electrochemical Society Active Member.
+zE-mail: cxw31@psu.edu
+in a large Li-ion battery, a multi-dimensional (multi-D) battery model
+needs to be validated against not only overall cell performance, but
+also against spatially resolved data.
+Therefore, it is of great importance to experimentally measure
+such critical parameters as current density, temperature and SOC, in
+Li-ion batteries locally, in order to reveal insight about their distribu-
+tion characteristics and to provide spatially resolved data for multi-D
+model validation. Considering that distribution of those parameters is
+transient in nature, in-situ measurement is desired.
+Prior research on this important topic has been very limited. As
+an important indicator of Li-ion battery performance and aging, local
+SOC received relatively more attention. Maire et al. 16 developed an
+in-situ colorimetry method to map SOC distribution based on the fact
+that electrode materials change color upon lithium intercalation. They
+demonstrated the application of this method in an aged graphite elec-
+trode and observed highly non-uniform SOC distribution. Liu et al. 17
+and Nanda et al.18 respectively used X-ray micro-diffraction (μXRD)
+and micron-resolution Raman spectroscopy for ex-situ mapping of the
+SOC distribution, both in the through-plane and in-plane directions
+of electrodes. As a powerful and non-invasive imaging technique,
+neutron radiography has great potential for in-situ mapping of SOC
+in Li-ion batteries, and the application was demonstrated by Butler
+et al.19 and Siegel et al. 20 As for local temperature measurement, Lee
+et al. 21 embedded two micro temperature sensors into a Li-ion bat-
+tery and observed slightly higher internal temperature than surface
+temperature during 1 C charge/discharge. Forgez et al. 22 inserted a
+thermocouple into the center of a 26650 Li-ion battery cell by drilling
+to access the central hole of jelly roll. The temperature measured
+by the internal thermocouple was compared with that measured on
+the cell surface. Obvious temperature difference was observed during
+pulse charge/discharge at high C rate. Forgez et al. 22 also recorded
+surface temperatures with infrared thermography, which showed very
+slight temperature difference at different locations on the surface. By
+developing a small pouch cell with multiple working electrodes and
+multiple layers of separators, Ng et al. 23 demonstrated measurement
+of local current density across the thickness of electrode and observed
+non-uniform current distribution even at very low C rate (C/37 in their
+study).
+While some progress has been made in experimentally observing
+the non-uniform distribution in SOC, temperature or current den-
+sity in Li-ion batteries, most work remained qualitative or provided
+few measurement results. Some methods were restricted to surface
+measurement16 or ex situ. 17,18 To date, in-situ spatially resolved ex-
+perimental data that can be readily used for model validation remain
+elusive.
+
+Journal of The Electrochemical Society, 160 (4) A610-A615 (2013) A611
+Figure 1. Schematic of the experimental pouch cell with a segmented positive
+electrode.
+In this work, current distribution is measured in-situ along the
+length of an electrode sheet using a newly developed pouch cell with
+a segmented positive electrode. Current distribution under different
+discharge C rates and ambient temperatures is systematically inves-
+tigated. Based on the current distribution data, information of SOC
+distribution during operation is also obtained. To our best knowledge,
+the present work is the ﬁrst attempt to measure current distribution
+in-situ and provide spatially-resolved data for model validation.
+Experimental
+Experimental cell.— As schematically shown in Fig. 1, the exper-
+imental cell consists of one negative electrode (with active material
+coated on both sides of a Cu foil), two layers of separators, and multi-
+ple positive electrode segments (10 in this study, with active material
+coated on both sides of an Al foil). The negative electrode has one tab,
+which serves as the negative terminal of the cell, while every positive
+electrode segment has two tabs (with only one used in this study, as
+s h o w ni nF i g .1). The negative electrode and separators are folded in
+a serpentine manner, with one positive electrode segment sandwiched
+inside each fold.
+In the experimental cell, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and graphite
+are used as positive and negative electrode materials. Celgard 2320
+PP/PE/PP trilayer membrane (20 um thick)24 is used as separator. The
+electrolyte is 1.2 M LiPF6 in EC:EMC:PC (45:50:5 v%). The thickness
+of active material coating (each side) is 64 um in positive electrode
+and 43 um in negative electrode. The thickness of Al foil is 15 um and
+that of Cu foil is 10 um. Every positive electrode segment is 150 mm
+long and 56.5 mm wide (i.e. the coating area). The negative electrode
+is ∼1.8 m long. Many more details of electrode fabrication are given
+elsewhere25 and thus not repeated here. The electrode-separator sand-
+wich is assembled in a pouch cell. After electrolyte ﬁlling, the pouch
+cell is sealed with one negative terminal and twenty positive terminals
+exposed to the outside.
+Experimental system.— Fig. 2 shows a schematic of the experi-
+mental system in this work. Note that the segmented cell is unfolded
+and simpliﬁed here for convenience of understanding. The 10 posi-
+tive electrode segments are connected in parallel to a bus wire, each
+through a shunt resistor (PL V7AL, 2 m/Omega1± 0.5%, Precision Resistor
+Co., USA) for local current sensing. By connecting the 10 positive
+electrode segments in parallel and making resistance from the posi-
+tive terminal bus to the Al tab uniform for each local channel, we can
+suppress the effects of Al foil on current distribution so as to focus on
+the effects of the negative Cu current collector. Such a conﬁguration
+is also representative of a prevailing battery design with continuous
+tab along the positive electrode sheet (as the Al foil is more resistive)
+and discrete tabs on the negative electrode sheet (as the Cu foil is less
+resistive). A low resistance meter (3560, Hioki, Japan) is used to en-
+sure that the resistance of shunt and connecting wires is the same for
+every channel (4.0 ± 0.1 m/Omega1in this study), and resistance of the bus
+wire is low enough to be negligible ( <0.1 m/Omega1). The 4 m/Omega1resistance
+of shunt and connecting wires introduced for current measurements
+is negligibly small as compared to the internal resistance of each cell
+segment (∼300 m/Omega1at room temperature).
+A battery tester (BT2000, Arbin Instruments, USA) is used to
+control the overall current/voltage of the experimental cell. A multi-
+channel data acquisition (DAQ) unit (34970A, Agilent Technologies,
+USA) is used to measure voltage drops across shunt resistors, which is
+then converted to local currents. Overall cell voltage is also recorded
+by the DAQ. All the data reported in this paper is recorded by the
+DAQ with a time interval of one second. To investigate the effect
+of the ambient temperature on current distribution, an environmental
+chamber (Tenney T10c, Thermal Product Solutions, USA) is used to
+control the ambient temperature during high- and low-temperature
+tests.
+Figure 2. Schematic of the experimental system (cell unfolded and simpliﬁed; not to scale; arrows schematically showing current ﬂow during discharge).
+
+A612 Journal of The Electrochemical Society, 160 (4) A610-A615 (2013)
+Figure 3. Cell performance at various discharge C rates at 21 ◦C.
+Test procedures.— Before every test, the battery tester and DAQ
+are started and rested for one hour, then the cell is fully charged at room
+temperature (21◦C) using a Constant Current-Constant V oltage (CC-
+CV) protocol (1.5 A, 3.6 V max, 0.05 A cutoff). Subsequently, the cell
+is rested for two hours (for test at 21◦C) or four hours (for tests at 45◦C
+and 0◦C), allowing open circuit voltage (OCV) and temperature of the
+cell to reach equilibrium before discharge. For tests under different
+discharge conditions, the cell is discharged at speciﬁed C rate (based
+on nominal capacity of 2.4 Ah) until its voltage drops to 2.7 V .
+Results and Discussion
+Overall cell performance.— Fig. 3 shows overall performance of
+the experimental cell during discharge at various C rates (C/5, C/2,
+1 C, 2 C and 4 C). The OCV performance is also shown, which is
+obtained by discharging the cell at C/10 intermittently with a rest pe-
+riod of one hour. As expected, the cell voltage and discharge capacity
+decrease with increasing C rate, which can be attributed to higher
+ohmic and kinetic overvoltage at higher current. The capacity at C/5
+discharge is around 2.4 Ah, which is used as nominal capacity. The
+OCV variation matches open circuit potential (OCP , vs Li/Li+)c h a r -
+acteristics of LFP 26 and graphite 27 very well, suggesting the OCV
+variation is mainly from the OCP variation of graphite since LFP has
+a very ﬂat OCP curve in a wide range.
+Current distribution during 1 C discharge.— Fig. 4 shows the
+measured current distribution during 1 C discharge at 21◦C. Note that
+local currents are made dimensionless after being normalized by the
+average current for convenient comparison among different cases. The
+discharge time is also made dimensionless for convenient comparison
+by using the cell SOC to indicate discharge progress. Average current
+(equal to the unity after normalization) and cell voltage are shown in
+the ﬁgure as reference. Fig. 5 shows dimensionless spatial distribu-
+tion of local currents at different levels of cell SOC, using the local
+currents data extracted from Fig. 4. It can be seen clearly from these
+two ﬁgures that current distribution is not uniform from beginning of
+discharge and evolves signiﬁcantly as discharge proceeds. Initially,
+segments closer to the negative terminal produce higher local currents
+than those farther away, i.e. I 1 > I2 > I3... >I10. As discharge con-
+tinues, local currents in segments with higher initial values generally
+decrease, while those with lower initial values increase, which leads to
+an entirely different pattern of current distribution near the end of dis-
+charge (I1 < I2 < I3...) .N o t et h a tI9 is almost always slightly higher
+than I 10 because segment 9 has slightly higher capacity than other
+segments (0.250 Ah vs 0.241 ± 0.004 Ah, obtained from integration
+of local currents in time during C/5 discharge).
+Figure 4. Local currents vs. cell state of charge (SOC) during 1 C discharge
+at 21◦C.
+The very non-uniform current distribution at the beginning of dis-
+charge can be attributed to the resistance of the negative current col-
+lector (10 um thick Cu foil, with resistance of ∼55 m/Omega1for the whole
+length of 1.8 m). As schematically shown in Fig. 2, current ﬂows
+in the Cu foil from the negative terminal to the other end, gradually
+decreases along the ﬂow direction as local currents enter the negative
+electrode. As the current ﬂows in, considerable potential drop along
+the Cu foil occurs due to its resistance. On the other hand, poten-
+tials of segments on the positive side (joint of shunt resistor with bus
+wire) are essentially equal due to negligible resistance of the bus wire.
+Consequently, the local overvoltage is smaller for segments farther
+from the negative terminal, thereby driving lower current according to
+electrochemical kinetics (e.g. Butler-V olmer Equation).28 Therefore,
+the farther a segment is from the negative terminal, the smaller the
+local overvoltage is, and the lower current it generates. Higher SOC
+remains in regions far away from the negative terminal.
+As discharge proceeds, the regions farther away from the negative
+terminal maintain higher SOC due to less current generation earlier
+and hence produce higher local currents. The dramatic variation of
+local currents during late stages of discharge can be attributed to the
+counteracting effects between potential drop along the Cu foil and
+the local SOC non-uniformity. The two effects counteract, tending to
+balance the current distribution. Therefore, local currents in segments
+Figure 5. Spatial current distribution at different cell SOC during 1 C dis-
+charge at 21◦C.
+
+Journal of The Electrochemical Society, 160 (4) A610-A615 (2013) A613
+Figure 6. Local currents vs. cell SOC during C/5 discharge at 21 ◦C.
+with higher initial values would decrease, while local currents in
+segments with lower initial values would increase. When the effect of
+local SOC non-uniformity overrides the effect of the ohmic potential
+drop along the Cu foil, in the case near the end of discharge, the current
+distribution would reverse in pattern, becoming entirely different from
+that at the beginning of discharge. See Figs. 4 and 5.
+Effects of C rate on current distribution.— C rate is an important
+parameter for Li-ion battery operation, which inﬂuences both perfor-
+mance and durability, so current distribution in the experimental cell
+is measured at various C rates (C/5, C/2, 1 C, 2 C and 4 C) to in-
+vestigate its effects. Results at C/5 and 4 C are shown in Fig. 6 and
+Fig. 7, respectively, for comparison with results at 1 C. It can be seen
+clearly that local currents spread less during lower C-rate discharge,
+indicating more uniform current distribution. This trend can be more
+clearly seen from Fig. 8, in which the differences between I 1 and
+I10 during different C rate discharge are plotted together. Segments 1
+and 10 are most apart along the negative current collector, and I 1 and
+I10 are most different, so their difference, i.e. the maximum /Delta1I, can
+be used to represent the non-uniformity of current distribution in the
+experimental cell.
+The effects of C-rate on current distribution again can be attributed
+to the opposing effects of potential drop along the Cu foil and the local
+SOC non-uniformity. During low C rate discharge (C/5), potential
+drop along the Cu foil is so small that the local current distribution
+Figure 7. Local currents vs. cell SOC during 4 C discharge at 21 ◦C.
+Figure 8. Maximum difference in local current during different C rate dis-
+charge at 21◦C.
+is controlled by local SOC non-uniformity. Indeed a wavy pattern,
+evident from Figs. 6 and 8, results, reﬂective of multiple plateaus
+and frequent slope changes seen in the OCV vs. SOC curve. On the
+other hand, during high C rate discharge (4 C) the potential drop
+along the Cu foil, amounting to ∼20 times larger than that during C/5
+discharge, dominates the local current distribution. This dominance
+by the ohmic potential drop creates smoothly varying patterns, as can
+be seen clearly from Fig. 8 for the cases of 1 C, 2 C and 4 C. We
+hypothesize that a battery operated in close vicinity to the equilibrium
+features a wavy current distribution while a battery operated far away
+from the equilibrium would exhibit a monotonic variation.
+Effects of ambient temperature on current distribution.— Ambi-
+ent temperature is another important operating parameter for Li-ion
+batteries. Fig. 9 and Fig. 10 show the current distribution at elevated
+temperature (45◦C) and lower temperature (0◦C) during 1 C discharge.
+Comparison with the results at 21 ◦C, as shown in Fig. 4, clearly in-
+dicates lower overall performance but more uniform current distri-
+bution at lower ambient temperature. This interesting phenomenon
+can be mainly attributed to the effects of temperature on the internal
+resistance of Li-ion battery cells, which includes the ohmic resistance
+(Ro), the charge transfer resistance (R ct) and the resistance of SEI
+(Rsei). Previous studies4,29 show that the charge transfer resistance and
+the SEI resistance increase dramatically at lower temperature while
+Figure 9. Local currents vs. cell SOC during 1 C discharge at 45 ◦C.
+
+A614 Journal of The Electrochemical Society, 160 (4) A610-A615 (2013)
+Figure 10. Local currents vs. cell SOC during 1 C discharge at 0 ◦C.
+the ohmic resistance change little. According to the previous studies,
+internal resistance of the experimental cell in this study would be
+much higher at 0◦C in comparison with that at 21 ◦C. As suggested in
+Fig. 2, higher charge transfer resistance and SEI resistance at lower
+temperature would make the effects of ohmic potential drop along
+the Cu foil less signiﬁcant on the current distribution. Therefore, the
+current distribution would be more uniform at lower temperature.
+Obviously, higher internal resistance would reduce the overall perfor-
+mance of the experimental cell due to higher overvoltage at the same
+current. The better overall performance yet more non-uniform current
+distribution at 45◦C agrees with the explanations as well.
+Note that the resistance of Cu foil is slightly lower at lower temper-
+atures (the temperature coefﬁcient of Cu resistivity is ∼0.4%◦C−1),30
+so the potential drop along the Cu foil is lower, which could also
+contribute to the more uniform current distribution at low tempera-
+tures. However, this effect is minor in comparison with the change of
+charge-transfer and SEI resistances with temperature.
+Local SOC distribution.— With information on local currents, lo-
+cal SOC during discharge can be calculated, providing additional data
+for model validation. Discharged capacity of every segment can be
+calculated by integrating local current in time from beginning of dis-
+charge. Then local SOC can be obtained by taking capacity of local
+segment during C/5 discharge as reference of SOC = 100%.
+Figure 11. Local SOC distribution at different cell SOC during 1 C discharge
+at 21◦C.
+Figure 12. Local SOC distribution at cutoff during different C rate discharge
+at 21◦C.
+Fig. 11 shows distribution of local SOC at different cell SOC during
+1 C discharge. As expected, the SOC distribution ﬁrst becomes more
+and more non-uniform as discharge proceeds due to the higher local
+currents closer to the negative terminal, and then the SOC distribution
+becomes less non-uniform as discharge approaches end of discharge
+due to the reversal of current distribution.
+It is interesting to note that the SOC distribution is still not uniform
+at cutoff for 1 C discharge. This phenomenon is even more obvious at
+higher C rates, as can be seen from Fig. 12, which shows SOC distri-
+bution at cutoff for different C rate discharge. For the 4 C discharge,
+local SOC of segment 1 is around 30%, while that of segment 10 is
+higher than 60%. Such highly non-uniform SOC distribution at cutoff
+signiﬁcantly under-utilizes the active materials loaded in the battery,
+thereby reducing its energy density. Indeed, the very high SOC of seg-
+ment 10 suggests that active materials in certain locations are largely
+under-utilized, a signiﬁcant waste of battery materials.
+Note that non-uniform SOC distribution at cutoff suggests non-
+uniform local OCV distribution, which causes internal balancing cur-
+rents when the cell is placed on open circuit after cutoff. The internal
+balancing currents were indeed observed in our experiments and a
+detailed study on this topic is underway, which will be reported in a
+future publication.
+Conclusions
+Current distribution in a Li-ion battery is measured in-situ for the
+ﬁrst time using a newly designed pouch cell with a segmented elec-
+trode sheet. Results show that current distribution is not uniform from
+the beginning of discharge and evolves dramatically as discharge pro-
+ceeds. Initially, segments closer to the negative terminal have higher
+local currents due primarily to the ohmic potential drop along the
+negative current collector. On the contrary, near the end of discharge,
+current distribution reverses in pattern, attributed to the effect of local
+SOC non-uniformity. Effects of C rate and ambient temperature on
+current distribution are investigated. It is found that current distribu-
+tion is more uniform at lower C rates and lower temperatures. The
+former can be attributed to lower potential drop along the current col-
+lector foil at lower C rate, and the latter can be mainly attributed to
+the cell’s higher internal resistance at lower temperature. SOC distri-
+bution during discharge is also obtained based on the information on
+local currents. It is found that SOC distribution is uneven during dis-
+charge, even at cutoff during high C rate discharge, clearly indicating
+under-utilization of active materials.
