+# Capillary-relay copper removal from solid steel scrap
+
+**15 October 2026, Australia/Brisbane. Status: UNTESTED CONSTRUCTION; no demonstrated capability advantage. Novelty: UNKNOWN.** This report proposes an operation for a consequential but carefully restricted feed: fragmented steel with copper *attached to or exposed at its surface* before remelting. It does not purport to remove copper already dissolved through millimetre-thick steel. No laboratory experiment was performed here.
+
+## Decision and physical access
+
+Copper carried into an electric-arc-furnace (EAF) melt cannot be removed by routine steel refining, and it limits high-grade flat-steel recycling. Daehn, Serrenho and Allwood report about 0.4 wt% Cu in typical shredded end-of-life scrap versus below 0.1 wt% for many flat products, and note that hammer shredding entangles copper wiring with steel. Their assessment reports an older estimate that 90% of contaminating Cu was surface-associated for the particular scrap feedstocks studied; it explicitly warns that this need not cover Cu already alloyed into recycled steel. A 2018 Japanese material-flow study independently distinguishes externally mixed Cu from alloyed Cu and finds that the latter contribution had risen in its studied system. Thus the starting measurement must quantify *accessible metallic Cu mass*, not merely total elemental Cu. [Daehn et al. 2019](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11663-019-01537-9); [Nakamura et al. 2018](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/tetsutohagane/104/8/104_TETSU-2018-009/_article/-char/en).
+
+The physical affordance is a temperature window above Cu's melting point and below steel's, together with differential surface energy. Daehn et al. directly saw Cu liquate on solid low-carbon steel, sometimes as a stable droplet; on medium-carbon steel, scale blistering and oxide/metal gaps allowed the liquid to spread under scale and into grain boundaries. This makes simple preferential melting a serious existing method but also identifies its failure mode: Cu stays attached or disappears under scale. A 2026 experiment on *clean, porous iron in vacuum* directly measured molten-Cu wetting (contact angle about 9 ± 5 degrees at 1100 °C) and rapid infiltration from finite droplets (reported 420 ± 50 mm/s at 1150 °C). It demonstrates the collector interaction, **not** transfer from heterogeneous scrap, a Cu–Sn alloy, an oxidized foam, or a micrometre-thin interfacial film. [Daehn et al. 2019, wetting experiments](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11663-019-01578-0); [Zhevnenko and Petrov 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.surfin.2026.108970).
+
+## Proposed operation: a capillary relay during scrap preheat
+
+Build a short hot stage upstream of an EAF or as an experimental batch cell. Classify a lot by composition, carbon level, surface oxide and externally attached Cu fraction using representative sectioning plus bulk ICP/OES or equivalent assays. Preheat steel pieces to a calibrated temperature just above the Cu-rich phase liquidus while keeping the steel solid, in a controlled low-oxidation-potential gas. A mechanically compliant, replaceable porous-Fe cassette is reduced/cleaned separately, then briefly pressed against the liquated Cu-bearing surfaces and withdrawn. Connected pores pull accessible liquid Cu into the cassette by capillarity. Repeated contact positions, not higher heating, address irregular fragment geometry. Copper-filled cassettes leave as a separate Cu–Fe feedstock; their regeneration or sale is part of the process cost. The steel proceeds to the EAF only if a representative post-treatment assay clears the Cu specification.
+
+The process is **selective by location and phase, not by a claim that Fe and Cu have magically different chemistry in the melt**. The steel core remains solid. On low-carbon pieces a thin oxide may reduce adhesion of Cu to the base while the freshly prepared Fe collector is Cu-wetting. This is a difficult two-surface state to maintain at a common gas potential; it is a design hypothesis requiring direct measurement. For medium-carbon or heavily scaled scrap, a shallow mechanical scale-opening step may expose trapped Cu, but this can tear the steel, oxidize Fe, or drive Cu inward. These feeds require a separate pass/fail gate; do not average them into a successful low-carbon result.
+
+**Measurement and control are part of the operation.** Calibrate furnace pyrometry against embedded thermocouples; track O\(_2\) potential/dew point; use high-speed optical/thermal imaging on witness contacts (the observation method is demonstrated for porous-Fe melt uptake in the 2026 study) and a calibrated four-terminal conductance change across each cassette as *candidate* fill signals. A Cu-filled Fe pore should add a parallel conductive path, but temperature, Fe oxidation, pressure and solid-state contact may imitate it. Therefore those signals set contact time and cassette replacement only after blinded calibration against weighed and sectioned cassettes; they never certify product purity. Periodic destructive cross sections of scrap and cassette, ICP/OES Cu/Fe mass balances, and EAF melt assays are the independent verification. The controller stops or diverts a lot if Cu uptake stalls, Fe loss increases, or accessible-Cu uncertainty is too large. No opaque classifier is needed.
+
+The mechanism can be expressed by an ideal pore competition condition. For a cylindrical collector pore of radius \(r\), molten-Cu surface tension \(\gamma\), dynamic wetting angle \(\theta_w\), and viscosity \(\mu\), its ideal capillary pressure is \(2\gamma\cos\theta_w/r\). Transfer from the scrap requires this pressure to exceed the effective retention/pinning pressure on the base plus any oxide-film rupture or entrance barrier. For an ideal isolated pore, Lucas–Washburn predicts \(\ell^2\simeq (\gamma r\cos\theta_w/2\mu)t\); real porous-Fe data themselves show that dynamic contact angles and geometry matter, so this is a *design inequality*, not a predicted production speed. The missing, load-bearing quantity is the probability that a Cu-bearing surface actually forms a liquid bridge to an unsaturated, clean pore before it wets a steel grain boundary or becomes trapped beneath scale. [Zhevnenko and Petrov 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.surfin.2026.108970); [Daehn et al. 2019](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11663-019-01578-0).
+
+## Exact mass gate and a failed broader mechanism
+
+For an illustrative one-tonne lot at 0.4 wt% Cu, the initial Cu mass is 4 kg. If \(R\) kg Cu and \(L\) kg Fe are removed, the output assay is
+
+\[
+ c_{\mathrm{out}}=\frac{4-R}{1000-R-L}.
+\]
+
+Meeting \(c_{\mathrm{out}}\leq 0.001\) requires \(R\geq(3+0.001L)/0.999\). With zero Fe loss this is **3.003 kg Cu**, or 75.08% of all incoming Cu. Let \(f\) be the fraction of Cu in an accessible surface phase and \(\eta\) the *measured* fraction of that phase captured. Necessarily \(f\eta\geq0.7508\) before any Fe loss. If \(f=0.90\), the required capture is \(\eta\geq0.8342\); if \(f\leq0.75\), the 0.1 wt% goal is impossible for any surface-only device. These are arithmetic consequences of the stated feed and target, not empirical efficiencies. The accompanying `bounds.py` prints the calculations.
+
+The initially broader idea was to oxidize Fe so that Cu dissolved in steel is rejected as a surface liquid, then wick it away. High-temperature experiments do show Cu enrichment at the oxide/steel interface near 1100–1150 °C, and an older oxidation paper found Cu in scale as well as at the interface. However, that access is extremely shallow at practical hold times. Majima and Mitani measured the Cu lattice tracer diffusivity in austenite as \(D_l=4.16\times10^{-4}\exp[-305{,}000/(RT)]\,\mathrm{m^2s^{-1}}\). At 1150 °C, direct substitution gives \(D_l\approx2.66\times10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m^2s^{-1}}\) and \(\sqrt{2D_lt}\approx4.4\) micrometres in one hour. A deliberately generous ideal absorbing-boundary calculation for a 1-mm slab exposed on both sides gives about 0.7% of initially uniform lattice Cu reaching a face in that hour. Grain boundaries, advancing oxidation, and local liquid penetration change the real profile, but they do not justify claiming bulk de-coppering from this lattice-only estimate. If the front instead exposes bulk Cu by oxidizing successive Fe layers and no deeper diffusion helps, recovering 75% of uniformly alloyed Cu requires oxidizing roughly 75% of the Fe, then handling or reducing that oxide. The useful redesign is therefore to restrict the operation to attached or already exposed Cu and acquire \(f\) for every lot. [Majima and Mitani 1978](https://doi.org/10.2320/matertrans1960.19.663); [high-temperature oxidation experiment, 2026](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12897733/); [2004 Cu distribution experiment](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/isijinternational1989/44/9/44_9_1576/_article/-char/en).
+
+The ideal sink calculation is only a mechanism check. It assumes constant \(D_l\), a planar uniform slab, two perfectly absorbing faces, and no moving oxide front. It is **not** a measured bound on real scrap, which has variable phase, geometry, grain boundaries and Cu-bearing attachments. Its purpose is to expose the invalid jump from observing a surface Cu film to claiming removal of alloyed bulk Cu.
+
+## Strongest equally informed comparators
+
+The production comparator is the best available combination of pre-shred/fragmentation, magnetic/density/optical separation and manual or automated removal, followed by EAF blending to specification. This cannot be dismissed as merely conceptual: Koinig et al. report a 2026 industrial trial of optical ejection on rusty post-shredder material above 3 t/h. In a 490-kg validation run, their retained 452.98-kg fraction contained 0.42 kg of *visibly* Cu-bearing particles, and they report 99.907 wt% of retained particles without visible Cu. They also report 33.84 kg of iron co-ejected with the reject fraction. These are substantial operational results, but **99.907 wt% visibly Cu-free particles is not a bulk elemental-Cu assay or a claim that 0.1 wt% melt Cu was reached**. An equally informed dry-sorting line given the same feed and assay might be cheaper and faster than any hot contact process; the decisive comparison includes both residual Cu and Fe yield. [Koinig et al. 2026, industrial trial and mass breakdown](https://doi.org/10.3390/pr14050746).
+
+The direct closest physical comparator is **preferential Cu melting followed by mechanical shaking or molten-salt assisted removal**, with the same feed characterization, temperature profile, oxygen control and post-assay. Daehn et al. already proposed precisely that physics and observed the wetting/entrapment problem. A capillary cassette wins only if it collects the same accessible Cu at lower total cost, Fe loss and contamination, or reaches Cu that optimized shaking cannot access. [Daehn et al. 2019 comparative assessment](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11663-019-01537-9); [Daehn et al. 2019 wetting study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11663-019-01578-0).
+
+The strongest immersion comparator for irregular pieces is a hot extraction bath, especially sulfide matte or molten Al, because it contacts surfaces a pressed foam may miss. A primary 1991 molten-Al study reported externally Cu-contaminated solid scrap becoming Cu-free after 5–10 min at about 745 °C, but the downstream Al carryover must be charged. A reported sulfur-matte pilot on copper tubing wrapped around steel rods removed the attached Cu in minutes at 900–1000 °C, but Fe oxidation and sulfur control must be charged. Daehn et al.'s assessment estimates approximately 20 kg Al adhering per tonne of steel in one Al-extraction route and 20–30 kWh/t extra desulfurization for one matte route; these are *model estimates from specified routes*, not measured universal constants. The capillary proposal must beat the best of these after matched feed preparation and full system accounting, not an artificially weak no-treatment baseline. [Iwase and Tokinori 1991](https://doi.org/10.1002/srin.199101282); [sulfur-matte primary report](https://p2infohouse.org/ref/25/24371.pdf); [Daehn et al. 2019](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11663-019-01537-9).
+
+Oxidation and machining of Cu-rich *steel surfaces* have also already been proposed and tested for hot-shortness mitigation. That is not the same feed as attached copper on irregular scrap, but it defeats any claim that creating and removing an oxidized Cu-rich skin is in itself new. [Yeşiltepe and Şeşen 2021](https://hrcak.srce.hr/246101). The 2026 Landi–Sridhar–De Moor paper also reports a mass-balance oxidation model for separated Cu layer thickness, so the mass-balance insight alone has unknown priority. Its full methods were not acquired here. [Primary article DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/srin.202501128).
+
+## Full-resource ledger and decisive test
+
+No end-to-end resource measurement exists for this construction. A valid comparison must record per tonne of *accepted, specification-grade steel*, including rejected lots:
+
+| Resource or loss | Proposed operation's charge | Matched comparator's charge |
+|---|---|---|
+| Acquisition and preparation | Statistical sampling, sectioning/assay of external versus alloyed Cu, fragmentation/cleaning, carbon/oxide map; uncertainty and rejected lots | Same information and equivalent feed conditioning |
+| Heat and atmosphere | Sensible heat to >Cu liquidus, holding/radiation and transfer losses, gas supply/purification, oxygen/dew-point control; credit recovered preheat only when measured | Full heat, bath or mechanical energy, atmosphere and transfer losses |
+| Collector and product | Fabrication, cleaning/reduction, pore degradation, Fe foam mass, captured-Cu grade, replacement/regeneration and Cu recovery from Cu–Fe cassette | Shaking/salt losses or Al/matte make-up, regeneration, disposal and product recovery |
+| Steel quality | Fe oxidation, fines/dust, added collector fragments or Cu penetration, residual Cu/Sn/S/Al, yield and downstream rolling defects | Same downstream assays and steel yield |
+| Reliability/scale | Contact probability across irregular fragments, throughput, cassette saturation, fouling, maintenance, off-spec diversion and unobserved buried Cu | Equal throughput and off-spec/rework treatment |
+
+An ideal pore-volume capacity calculation gives \(M_{\rm Cu,cap}=M_{\rm Fe,foam}[\phi/(1-\phi)](\rho_{\rm Cu}/\rho_{\rm Fe})\xi\), where \(\phi\) is open porosity and \(\xi\in[0,1]\) is *actual* pore filling. It is only a sizing ceiling. The dominant uncertainty is not whether enough void volume can be made; it is whether copper reaches that void from each real scrap fragment without excess Fe loss or Cu penetration.
+
+**Fatal test:** Before any pilot claim, randomize real shredded scrap lots spanning low/medium carbon, rust/oxide, small Cu wires, Cu-plated pieces and pieces with independently measured alloyed Cu. Pre-register a target below 0.1 wt% Cu in the accepted EAF melt, at least 90% Fe yield, complete Cu/Fe/Sn mass closure within pre-specified assay uncertainty, and noninferior throughput and total energy/material cost to the best optimized comparator on the same lots. Run (i) thermal/preheat-only, (ii) optimized preferential melting plus mechanical/salt removal, (iii) hot immersion if viable, and (iv) capillary relay with live signals and post-assay. Blind downstream bulk Cu assays and metallographic checks for grain-boundary Cu, scale entrapment and steel rolling defects. The first coupon-scale gate is simpler: show directly that a clean Fe collector removes Cu from an actual oxidized low-carbon steel contact **against the base's wetting/pinning**, then repeat for medium-carbon, Cu–Sn and dirty surfaces. If no favorable pressure-transfer window exists, the capillary mechanism fails even though clean Cu droplets imbibe clean porous Fe in vacuum. If the coupon works but \(f\eta\) cannot meet the mass gate or the optimized comparator is cheaper, the operation still fails as a consequential capability.
+
+## Evidence/provenance boundary
+
+**Established literature inspected:** the 2019 Cambridge assessment's full accessible article and wetting-study methods/discussion, the 2026 industrial optical-ejection trial's abstract/results/mass breakdown, the 1978 diffusion abstract and measured equation, the 2018 Japanese material-flow abstract, the 2004 oxidation abstract, the 2021 machining abstract, the 1991 Al-extraction abstract, and search-indexed author/publisher text for the 2026 porous-Fe infiltration and oxidation studies. The sulfur-matte report's indexed test/result excerpts were inspected; its full PDF was not independently audited. The 2026 analytical oxidation model was seen only as an abstract/metadata summary, not full methods.
+
+**Original derivation here:** the Cu/Fe mass gate, required \(f\eta\), the diffusion substitution and ideal-sink consequence, and the conditional capillary-transfer inequality. `bounds.py` runs only arithmetic on stated inputs; it is not a physical simulation or empirical result.
+
+**Untested hypotheses:** a clean porous Fe cassette can outcompete the actual scrap surface for liquid Cu under one controlled atmosphere; collector-fill signals remain interpretable; heterogeneous contact coverage and Cu–Fe product handling can scale without an adverse resource ledger. The literature proves none of these. The operation is a specific experimental proposal with a strong falsifier, not a demonstrated breakthrough or novelty-cleared invention.

+"""Reproduce illustrative mass and lattice-diffusion checks in REPORT.md.
+
+Literature input for D_l: Majima and Mitani (1978), DOI

+illustrative 0.4 and 0.1 wt% values discussed by Daehn et al. (2019), DOI
+10.1007/s11663-019-01537-9. No physical process is simulated.
+"""
+
+import math
+
+
+def required_copper_removal(feed_mass_kg, feed_cu_fraction, target_cu_fraction,
+                            iron_loss_kg=0.0):
+    """Solve (Cu_in-R)/(M_in-R-L) <= target for R."""
+    return (feed_mass_kg * (feed_cu_fraction - target_cu_fraction)
+            + target_cu_fraction * iron_loss_kg) / (1 - target_cu_fraction)
+
+
+def copper_lattice_diffusivity(temp_c):
+    gas_constant = 8.314462618  # J mol^-1 K^-1
+    return 4.16e-4 * math.exp(-305_000 / (gas_constant * (temp_c + 273.15)))
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    feed_mass = 1000.0
+    initial_cu = feed_mass * 0.004
+    removal = required_copper_removal(feed_mass, 0.004, 0.001)

+    print(f"Fraction of all Cu: {removal / initial_cu:.6f}")
+    print(f"Capture if accessible fraction is 0.90: {removal / (0.90 * initial_cu):.6f}")

+# Adversarial audit of the baseline covariance chemistry certificate
+
+**Disposition:** The proposed inequalities are mathematically correct for a strictly positive deterministic mass-action state when **every hidden reversible pair is individually balanced at the baseline**, (Q) is the consistently normalized full-species infinitesimal jump covariance of those pairs, and the stated exponent bound (M) holds for every hidden complex. The useful zero criterion is exact under those assumptions. Baseline stationarity, baseline covariance, and even separately observed total forward/backward jump rates do **not** establish the individual-balance premise. It is therefore a conditional certificate for a trusted equilibrium hidden class, not a model-free way to dismiss unknown side reactions in a driven manufacturing reactor. Novelty and practical advantage are unknown.
+
+## Algebra and exact quantifiers
+
+Write (s_r=\beta_r-\alpha_r), (a_r^+(c)=a_r^-(c)=w_r>0), and (c'=c\odot e^h). Define
+
+\[
+\theta_r(h)=\int_0^1\exp\big((1-t)\alpha_r\cdot h+t\beta_r\cdot h\big)\,dt.
+\]
+
+Then (e^{-M}\leq\theta_r\leq e^M) and (F_H(c')=-\sum_r w_r\theta_r s_r(s_r\cdot h)). Consequently, with (Q=2\sum_r w_rs_rs_r^\top),
+
+\[
+|z\cdot F_H(c')|\leq\frac{e^M}{2}\sqrt{(z^\top Qz)(h^\top Qh)},\qquad
+\frac{e^{-M}}2 h^\top Qh\leq-h\cdot F_H(c')\leq\frac{e^M}2 h^\top Qh.
+\]
+
+The factor (1/2) is right. Since all (w_r>0), (Q_h=0\) iff (s_r\cdot h=0\) for **each** hidden pair. Under individual baseline balance, this makes each pair balanced at (c'), hence (F_H(c')=0). Conversely, if (Q_h>0), (-h\cdot F_H(c')>0), so (F_H(c')\neq0). The zero equivalence does not need (M); the nonzero magnitude bounds do.
+
+## Baseline-indistinguishable counterexample when individual balance is unacquired
+
+At (c=(A,B)=(1,1)), consider two open, reversible, mass-action pairs:
+
+| Pair | Forward rate | Reverse rate | (s) |
+|---|---:|---:|---|
+| (\varnothing\rightleftharpoons A) | (2) | (A) | ((1,0)) |
+| (B\rightleftharpoons A+B) | (B) | (2AB) | ((1,0)) |
+
+The individual currents at baseline are (+1,-1); the *aggregate* forward and reverse event rates are both (3). Thus the complete observed species drift is zero and the baseline jump covariance is (Q=6e_Ae_A^\top). Take (h=(0,\log2)), hence (c'=(1,2)) and (Q_h=0). The first current remains (+1), the second becomes (-2), and (F_H(c')=-e_A), directly violating a zero-flux conclusion if aggregate stationarity were substituted for pairwise balance. The stated exponent premise even holds with (M=\log2); only individual baseline balance fails.
+
+An individually balanced comparator with the *same two reaction complexes* and forward/reverse rates (3/2,3/2) for each pair has the **same** aggregate (+A,-A) rates (3,3), drift zero, and (Q=6e_Ae_A^\top) at baseline. After (B\to2), its drift remains zero. Hence an arbitrarily accurate observation of the full baseline species jump process at that one state cannot distinguish the two mechanisms if reaction identity is hidden. [Exact rational replay](chemistry_counterexample.py) also finds a sign failure: at (A=11/10,B=1/4), the cancelling-current network has (F_A=3/5), so (-h\cdot F_H=-(3/5)\log(11/10)<0) while (Q_h>0). The advertised dissipative lower bound cannot be extended to merely stationary hidden networks.
+
+For context, [Feinberg's primary conditions for detailed balancing](https://doi.org/10.1016/0009-2509(89)85124-3) explicitly require rate-constant structure beyond stationarity; [Müller and Joshi's primary graph-theoretic paper](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11538-020-00792-1) distinguishes detailed from complex balance and gives stationary non-detailed-balanced examples. I inspected Feinberg's abstract and the Müller–Joshi abstract, introduction, and example passages; the concrete counterexample above is my own.
+
+## Salvage with a paid nonequilibrium-current budget
+
+If individual balance is unavailable, write (w_r=(a_r^++a_r^-)/2), (j_r=a_r^+-a_r^-), and (\bar e_r=(e^{\alpha_r\cdot h}+e^{\beta_r\cdot h})/2). The exact identity is
+
+\[
+F_H(c')=-\sum_r w_r\theta_r s_r(s_r\cdot h)+\sum_r j_r s_r\bar e_r.
+\]
+
+If the hidden aggregate is stationary at (c), so (\sum_r j_rs_r=0), the extra term is (\sum_r j_rs_r(\bar e_r-1)). Therefore one can add the explicit uncertainty term
+
+\[
+|z\cdot F_H(c')|\leq\frac{e^M}{2}\sqrt{Q_zQ_h}+(e^M-1)\sum_r|j_r(z\cdot s_r)|.
+\]
+
+This valid extension exposes the acquisition burden: (Q) alone does not bound the last term tightly when invisible currents cancel. A verified bound on absolute hidden pair currents or perturbation responses must be purchased. In the counterexample (Q_h=0) but the residual term is nonzero.
+
+## Physical acquisition, strongest comparator, and decisive test
+
+- **Channel premise:** A production reactor often has chemostatted reagents, fuels, catalysts and byproducts. Its net stationary composition does not certify detailed balance of unknown side reactions. Pair-resolved forward/reverse rates or a justified closed-equilibrium class plus a complete thermodynamic mechanism are needed. An apparently reversible arrow is insufficient.
+- **Full covariance:** (Q=2\sum wss^\top) is a conditional, infinitesimal covariance in molecule-count units when (w) is events/time. If (c) denotes concentration and (w) concentration flux, observed concentration covariance rate is (Q/V) for volume (V); normalization must be explicit. Finite-frame imaging adds detector noise, missed fast events, transport and changing state. Projected observables (y=Px) provide (PQP^\top), not generally (Q_h) or (Q_z). Known channels must be separated to get hidden (Q). Total (Q\succeq Q_{\rm hidden}) gives conservative **upper** bounds for absolute flux and dissipation under detailed balance, but not the stated lower dissipation bound; its zero test is stronger than hidden balance and is not equivalent to it.
+- **Exponent premise:** (M\geq\max_r\{|\alpha_r\cdot h|,|\beta_r\cdot h|\}) requires a bound on every hidden reactant/product complex, or a direct upper bound on their activity changes. Even under pairwise detailed balance, a hidden (nB\rightleftharpoons A+nB) pair at (c=(1,1)) has the same baseline (Q=2e_Ae_A^\top) for every (n) when both rates equal one, but after (A,B\to2A,2B) its flux is (-2^n e_A). Unknown spectator order makes a fixed (M) unavailable. At low copy number, stochastic propensities use falling factorials and the exact exponential shift needs replacement or a large-volume limit.
+- **Precision and cost:** Finite data cannot prove (Q_h=0) exactly. If a single event type with known projected jump (d=s\cdot h\) has zero observed events over time (T), an ideal 95% upper event-rate bound is about (3/T), giving (Q_h\lesssim3d^2/T) for that type; unobserved channels and detector efficiency worsen it. Acquiring (Q) at a held baseline requires preparation, state feedback, calibration, event bandwidth, repeated trajectories and volume normalization. The full-resource comparator is direct measurement of target-composition drift/product flux and conventional network identification with the same access, if the target can be safely prepared. +## Four conditional bounds and their physical meaning
+
+**1. Report strength versus disturbance.** If photons from two candidate states are Poisson with rates (Lr_0,Lr_1), where (L) is excitation scale and background is included, an observation lasting (T) has
+
+\[
+D_{\rm KL}(P_1\Vert P_0)=LT\{r_1\log(r_1/r_0)+r_0-r_1\}=LTk.
+\]
+
+For equal prior odds, the optimal classification error is at least \(\tfrac14 e^{-LTk}\). Thus error at most \(\epsilon<1/4\) requires \(LT\geq\log(1/(4\epsilon))/k\). If illumination independently produces a damaging lesion with hazard \(dL\), the reporter-induced lesion probability at this necessary exposure is at least \(1-\exp[-d\log(1/(4\epsilon))/k]\). This is a **model bound**, not a measured (d/k), and photoprotection can change both rates. Scheckenbach's bleaching/ROS and ROXS rescue show why same-substrate calibration is necessary. More decisively, if an intact frame and a frame with an unlabelled interior break produce the same observation law, (k=0): increasing illumination cannot certify structural integrity. Dynamic imager exchange can diagnose a damaged label or available docking site; it need not diagnose every backbone lesion.
+
+**2. Protected information versus repair access.** For a single repairable structural site, let damage occur at rate \(\lambda\) and repair at rate \(\mu\). A protective layer multiplies them by \(a\) and \(r\), respectively. Under the two-state constant-rate model its stationary intact fraction is \(r\mu/(a\lambda+r\mu)\). It improves over the uncoated fraction \(\mu/(\lambda+\mu)\) exactly when \(r>a\). A barrier can therefore coexist with repair when it excludes a damaging species more than it excludes the repair species. Eklund measured one favorable geometry: protruding handles remained accessible while buried biotin attachment suffered. This does **not** measure (r) for a damage-exposed scaffold toehold, a large enzyme, or an interior template. A protected route/template must remain physically legible to the reaction at the damaged site; otherwise apparent retention is merely slower damage. The key experiment must measure (a,r) on the *same coated 12HB and same challenge*, not splice together the Ponnuswamy and Eklund magnitudes.
+
+**3. Measurement versus action latency.** Let a lesion become irreparable at hazard \(\gamma\). Assume damage arrival phase is uniform relative to optical sampling period \(\Delta\), the diagnostic and reagent-delivery delay is \(\tau\), local repair completion is exponential at rate \(\mu\), and an event is detected with probability \(s\). Then the one-shot rescue probability is
+
+\[
+p_{\rm rescue}=s\,e^{-\gamma\tau}\frac{1-e^{-\gamma\Delta}}{\gamma\Delta}\frac{\mu}{\mu+\gamma}.
+\]
+
+This follows by averaging survival over the waiting time to the next observation, then competing repair against irreversible loss. Even with arbitrarily fast imaging, (p_{\rm rescue}\leq s e^{-\gamma\tau}\mu/(\mu+\gamma)\). The high-FBS result is qualitative evidence that an actual damage-rate regime can overwhelm this chemistry; it is **not** a measurement of \(\gamma\) or \(\mu\). Autonomous damage-exposed toehold recognition removes external image-to-command delay from the control loop, leaving imaging for quality assurance. That chemical gate is the published incumbent, so bypassing optical latency does not itself establish novelty.
+
+**4. Repair selectivity versus collateral action.** Suppose \(K\) defective sites each repair at hazard \(u\) and \(N\) initially intact sites each suffer an unacceptable false repair/action at hazard \(v\), independently while reagents remain present. In this model newly repaired sites are not susceptible to that harm before the run ends. The exact probability of all defects being repaired before the first harmful action is
+
+\[
+p_{\rm clean}=\prod_{j=1}^{K}\frac{ju}{ju+Nv}.
+\]
+
+For one defect, (N=100) vulnerable intact features, and 90% clean success, (u/v\geq900\). These are **illustrative assumed site counts and hazards**, not measured nanoruler selectivity. Identical-staple exchange at a good site may be harmless, so (v) must mean actual harmful collateral action, not every molecular binding event. Off-target staple replacement, dimerization, impaired docking or coating removal must be measured as collateral outcomes.

+"""Exact arithmetic check of baseline-indistinguishable mass-action networks."""
+
+from fractions import Fraction as F
+
+
+def rates(a: F, b: F, detailed_balance: bool) -> tuple[F, F]:
+    if detailed_balance:
+        # 0 <-> A and B <-> A+B, with both directions equal at A=B=1.
+        return F(3, 2) + F(3, 2) * b, F(3, 2) * a + F(3, 2) * a * b
+    return F(2) + b, a + F(2) * a * b
+
+
+for balanced in (False, True):
+    label = "pairwise balanced" if balanced else "cancelling currents"
+    forward, backward = rates(F(1), F(1), balanced)
+    print(label, "baseline (+,-,drift,Q_AA):", forward, backward,
+          forward-backward, forward+backward)
+    forward, backward = rates(F(1), F(2), balanced)
+    print(label, "B=2 (+,-,drift):", forward, backward,
+          forward-backward)
+    forward, backward = rates(F(11, 10), F(1, 4), balanced)
+    print(label, "A=11/10,B=1/4 drift:", forward-backward)

+"""Conditional competing-hazard selectivity threshold; no experimental rates."""
+
+from math import prod
+
+
+def exact_clean_repair_probability(defects: int, intact: int, repair_to_harm: float) -> float:
+    """All defects repair before any harm, under independent constant hazards."""
+    return prod(
+        j * repair_to_harm / (j * repair_to_harm + intact)
+        for j in range(1, defects + 1)
+    )
+
+
+def threshold(defects: int, intact: int, target: float) -> float:
+    low, high = 0.0, 1.0
+    while exact_clean_repair_probability(defects, intact, high) < target:
+        high *= 2
+    for _ in range(100):
+        midpoint = (low + high) / 2
+        if exact_clean_repair_probability(defects, intact, midpoint) < target:
+            low = midpoint
+        else:
+            high = midpoint
+    return high
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    for defects in (1, 9):
+        ratio = threshold(defects, 100, 0.9)
+        print(f"K={defects} N=100 target=0.9 a/b={ratio:.9f} "
+              f"P={exact_clean_repair_probability(defects, 100, ratio):.9f}")

+## Original derivation: make latent reversible reactions silent at the target
+
+Take N769's ideal isothermal, reversible elementary mass-action law with known detailed-balance reference `q`, known modeled reaction support, known positive baseline and independently multiplied forward/backward gates. For a modeled nonzero-current reaction, N769's factor `rho_r(h)` moves concentrations from `c` to `c'=c exp(h)`; setting `e'_r=e_r rho_r(h) gamma_r` makes `j'_r=gamma_r j_r` without knowing its absolute rate constant. N817 proves that `S diag(gamma) ker S ⊆ ker S` holds exactly when gamma is constant on each active circuit component of the *complete supplied* stoichiometry. Its fifth-edge counterexample shows the danger of an omitted, baseline-zero exchange.
+
+Now suppose a specified candidate set `H` of omitted reversible reactions has fixed, known internal stoichiometric columns `s_r≠0`, a compatible known `q`, positive gates, and **independently uncertain** absolute coefficients `kappa_r` varying over a box with nonempty interior. Let modeled reactions be exactly balanced at the chosen target. The unknown contribution to the internal steady-state residual is
+
+`R_H(c')=Σ_(r∈H) s_r e_r kappa_r[(c'/q)^(a_r)−(c'/q)^(b_r)]`.
+
+Because each coefficient varies independently, `R_H(c')=0` for **every** admissible coefficient vector if and only if each vector coefficient is zero. Since `s_r≠0` and `e_r>0`, this is equivalent to `s_r·log(c'/q)=0` for each hidden reaction. If each is known to be equilibrated at baseline and reservoirs are fixed, the target condition reduces to the linear constraints **`s_r·h=0`**. The forward direction follows by varying one `kappa_r` while holding the others fixed; the reverse follows by substitution. This is an elementary robust-identifiability result original to this report, under its exact independent-box and detailed-balance premises. If an omitted reaction has zero internal column but affects an external product, this only certifies *internal stationarity*, not the product objective.
+
+This does **not** contradict N817's maximal all-`ker S` theorem. N817 asks for stationarity for every possible current of the complete network. The present operation asks for stationarity of the particular physically admitted family in which each candidate hidden channel is zero at both endpoints. The condition can preserve distinct modeled pathway scales even if adding a hidden edge connects the complete network's circuit matroid. It needs an acquired candidate support and equilibrium relation; it cannot guard against arbitrary unseen reactions, driven cycles or unknown saturation. A hidden rate can still alter transient stability, noise, enzyme resource use and side products even when its net current vanishes at the target.
+
+### Exact two-pathway witness and equally informed incumbent
+
+Use FP's reservoirs `A=4`, `P=Q=1`, internal `B=C=2`, four modeled unit-rate reversible reactions `A↔B↔P` and `A↔C↔Q`, and baseline gates `(1/2,1,1/2,1)`. Choose `B'=C'=5/2` and gates `(9/8,9/8,3/8,3/8)`, still summing to 3. Then the modeled currents are exactly `(27/16,27/16,9/16,9/16)`, giving **3:1** product split; the hidden exchange current is zero for every `eta`. The target is stationary. For this linear toy alone, the Jacobian's negative quadratic form is `(9/4)v_B²+(3/4)v_C²+eta(v_B−v_C)²≥(3/4)||v||²`, so the target is globally exponentially stable in its stated time units. +"""Exact rational check of the scoped latent-exchange repair in REPORT.md.
+
+This is a finite fixture, not a proof of the general statement or a biochemical
+experiment. The four pathway rate coefficients are fixed to one; the fifth
+exchange coefficient eta is arbitrary and nonnegative.
+"""
+
+from fractions import Fraction as F
+
+
+def currents(B, C, gates, eta):
+    g1, g2, g3, g4 = gates
+    return (
+        g1 * (F(4) - B),
+        g2 * (B - F(1)),
+        g3 * (F(4) - C),
+        g4 * (C - F(1)),
+        eta * (B - C),
+    )
+
+
+def residual(js):
+    j1, j2, j3, j4, j5 = js
+    return (j1 - j2 - j5, j3 - j4 + j5)
+
+
+old_gates = (F(1, 2), F(1), F(1, 2), F(1))
+new_gates = (F(9, 8), F(9, 8), F(3, 8), F(3, 8))
+old = currents(F(2), F(2), old_gates, F(17, 19))
+new = currents(F(5, 2), F(5, 2), new_gates, F(17, 19))
+
+assert old == (F(1), F(1), F(1), F(1), F(0))
+assert new == (F(27, 16), F(27, 16), F(9, 16), F(9, 16), F(0))
+assert residual(old) == (F(0), F(0))
+assert residual(new) == (F(0), F(0))
+assert sum(old_gates) == sum(new_gates) == F(3)
+assert new[1] / new[3] == F(3)
+
+# For arbitrary eta>=0, v^T(-J)v = 9/4*v_B^2 + 3/4*v_C^2
+#                              + eta*(v_B-v_C)^2 >= 3/4*||v||_2^2.
+# Check an exact nonzero example, while the displayed identity proves the
+# uniform statement for this linear two-state fixture.
+eta = F(17, 19)
+vB, vC = F(7, 5), F(-2, 3)
+quadratic = F(9, 4) * vB**2 + F(3, 4) * vC**2 + eta * (vB - vC) ** 2
+assert quadratic >= F(3, 4) * (vB**2 + vC**2)
+
+print(f"baseline currents={old}; target currents={new}")
+print(f"gate sum={sum(new_gates)}; product ratio={new[1] / new[3]}")
+print("unknown exchange cancels identically when B=C=5/2")
+print("uniform Jacobian decay bound: at least 3/4 in this toy's time units")

+"""Floating-point diagnostics for the scoped three-snapshot ring calculation.
+
+This verifies formulas, not the universal affinity or reflection proof.  It uses
+only the Python standard library.  No laboratory or Monte Carlo data is used.
+"""
+
+import math
+
+
+def matmul(left, right):
+    return [
+        [sum(left[i][k] * right[k][j] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)]
+        for i in range(3)
+    ]
+
+
+def transition_by_uniformization(generator, time, escape, terms=50):
+    step = [
+        [float(i == j) + generator[i][j] / escape for j in range(3)]
+        for i in range(3)
+    ]
+    power = [[float(i == j) for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)]
+    result = [[0.0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]
+    weight = math.exp(-escape * time)
+    for n in range(terms):
+        for i in range(3):
+            for j in range(3):
+                result[i][j] += weight * power[i][j]
+        power = matmul(power, step)
+        weight *= escape * time / (n + 1)
+    return result
+
+
+q = 1 / 20
+t = 3 / 10
+s = 1 + q
+omega = math.sqrt(3) * (1 - q) / 2
+generator = [[-s, 1, q], [q, -s, 1], [1, q, -s]]
+transition = transition_by_uniformization(generator, t, s)
+g1 = transition[1][1] + transition[1][2]
+g2 = transition[2][1] + transition[2][2]
+a = (g1 + g2) / 2
+b = g1 * g2
+D = (2 / 3) * (a * a - b)
+
+closed_a = 2 / 3 + math.exp(-3 * s * t / 2) * math.cos(omega * t) / 3
+closed_D = 2 * math.exp(-3 * s * t) * math.sin(omega * t) ** 2 / 9
+assert abs(a - closed_a) < 1e-14
+assert abs(D - closed_D) < 1e-14
+assert all(abs(sum(row) - 1) < 1e-14 for row in transition)
+
+score_min = -a * (1 - a)
+score_range = max(a, 1 - a)
+floor = -math.log1p(-D / (-score_min)) / t
+target_sigma = (1 - q) * math.log(1 / q)
+independent_windows = math.ceil(
+    2 * score_range**2 * math.log(40) / D**2
+)
+
+print(f"a={a:.16g}")
+print(f"b={b:.16g}")
+print(f"D={D:.16g}")
+print(f"refined_floor={floor:.16g}")
+print(f"target_ring_sigma={target_sigma:.16g}")
+print(f"iid_window_planning_budget={independent_windows}")

+# Real-data audit: a measured SMA damper needs loading history to identify force
+
+**Status (15 October 2026): scoped empirical result reproduced; consequential new operation NOT_ACHIEVED.** A public, primary experimental release supports one quantitative information/control statement: in a large-scale shape-memory-alloy (SMA) damper under a specified cyclic displacement protocol, present displacement alone does not determine measured actuator force. A controller can infer a useful branch state from earlier readings of the *same* displacement sensor. The release does not test a new controller, establish improved structural safety, or show an advantage over a competent history-aware incumbent.
+
+## Source and inspected evidence
+
+Kolisch, Oflazgil and Klinkel (RWTH Aachen University), [Dataset of real-time hybrid simulation testing of multiple shape memory alloy based structural control devices](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17296336), record 17296336. I inspected the record description and its [one-page loading protocol](https://zenodo.org/records/17296336/files/Load_Protocol_v1.0.0.pdf?download=1), plus four actual CSVs inside [Data_v1.0.0.zip](https://zenodo.org/records/17296336/files/Data_v1.0.0.zip?download=1): `02_8wires_sin20mm_0p5Hz.csv`, `05_8wires_sin40mm_0p5Hz.csv`, `07_4wires_sin20mm_0p5Hz.csv`, and `09_4wires_sin20mm_0p5Hz_after_EQ.csv`. The related [2026 primary article](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jobe.2026.116572) was identified from the dataset and RWTH publication record; its full text was **not** used as evidence here.
+
+The record says the wires are 800 mm NiTi specimens from one batch, approximately 55.7% Ni, preconditioned for 20 strain-driven cycles to 5% at 0.5%/s. The 8-wire damper was driven sinusoidally to nominal ±20 mm at 0.5 Hz in source file 02. The file has 16,384 rows and three recorded columns: `Time` (s), `Actuator1_Disp` (mm), and `Actuator1_Force` (kN). Nominal sampling is 512 Hz; the CSV times are rounded decimals near 1/512 s. The imposed motion occupies about 0–20 s, followed by a rest segment to 32 s. The record describes MTS actuators with an integrated 500 kN load cell. The recorded displacement is the achieved actuator signal; the exact command trace, sensor calibration/uncertainty and controller latency are not supplied. The source explains that later real-time hybrid simulations include physical dampers coupled to a numerical structure; this audit uses the separate sinusoidal physical-damper tests, not a purported all-physical earthquake trial.
+
+The downloaded ZIP is 4,484,312 bytes. Its MD5 `da06b1056528e8429e7f64e3019cb17b` matches the Zenodo API file entry; SHA-256 is `8f32e7bdddbe2a262ed227df108a6fd05df87a5752ca1574f586b10a7748e929`. The protocol PDF's MD5 `fc4ad29433778e688abadccc47530099` also matches its record entry. [The saved metadata](source/zenodo_record.json) reports `cc-by-4.0`, while the page's usage prose says CC BY-SA 4.0; this discrepancy should be resolved before redistributing derived datasets. The scripts read the original ZIP directly.
+
+## Exact test and result
+
+The narrow claim is that a single-valued force rule \(g(x_t)\) cannot accurately represent both branches of this *measured* 8-wire, ±20 mm, 0.5 Hz trace at \(x=+10\) mm. For each of eight complete interior periods, 2–18 s, [audit.py](audit.py) finds the one rising and one falling crossing of +10 mm. It linearly interpolates force between the two adjacent recorded samples on each branch. This is a numerical interpolation of measurements, not an invented physical calibration.
+
+| Quantity, actuator 1 | Reproduced result |
+|---|---:|
+| Rising minus falling force at +10 mm, eight periods | 4.029–4.229 kN |
+| Mean branch separation | 4.133 kN |
+| Smallest paired, interpolated minimax error for any static \(g(10\text{ mm})\) | 2.015 kN |
+| Approximate mean \(\int F\,dx\) over those periods | 136.38 kN·mm = 136.38 J |
+
+The third line follows from the elementary inequality \(\max\{|g-y_\uparrow|,|g-y_\downarrow|\}\geq |y_\uparrow-y_\downarrow|/2\), applied to each interpolated pair. It is a bound on this *finite recorded trace* and interpolation procedure. No measurement uncertainty was provided, so it is not a calibrated physical lower confidence bound. The work integral is actuator force against measured motion; it is not electrical consumption, control cost, or necessarily heat dissipated, because a period's internal state need not close exactly.
+
+I also executed a causal, within-trace prediction check. A static lookup uses 0.5 mm displacement bins; a history lookup uses the identical bins plus the sign of \(x_i-x_{i-16}\). The latter reads only prior samples (16 samples = 31.25 ms at the nominal rate), with no extra physical sensor or future force. Both tables use per-bin training medians from four interior periods, 2–10 s. On the next four periods, 10–18 s, every one of 4,096 rows is covered. The static table has 81 bins and gives 1.465 kN mean absolute error; the branch-aware table has 162 bins and gives 0.223 kN, a 6.58-fold reduction. The branch predictor is a familiar hysteresis-aware baseline, not a new algorithm. Bin widths 0.25–1.0 mm and causal lookbacks 8–32 samples still give branch-aware errors 0.181–0.350 kN, while the static errors remain 1.465–1.482 kN; the exact numbers and settings are in [RESULTS.json](RESULTS.json). The split consists of consecutive cycles in **one run**; it does not establish cross-device, cross-rate or prospective performance.
+
+The [plot of a measured interior cycle](hysteresis_cycle.png) visibly shows the two force branches. Source file 05, the same 8-wire configuration at nominal ±40 mm and 0.5 Hz, provides a second measured check: its +10 mm gap is 5.119–6.689 kN across the same eight interior periods. The matched 4-wire, ±20 mm, 0.5 Hz files labeled before/after earthquake testing have mean branch gaps 1.955 and 1.844 kN, and approximate mean loop work 67.27 and 62.15 J. Those latter changes are observations under separate test runs; the files lack an environmental/fixture control sufficient to attribute them uniquely to earthquake exposure or material damage.
+
+## Operational meaning, equal-information comparator and costs
+
+The substrate stores loading-path state in its hysteresis. A feasible readout would combine measured actuator displacement with retained displacement history and use the inferred branch in force estimation or control. The decisive mathematical point is input nonidentifiability for a memoryless force law: no amount of static fitting to this trace can map the same +10 mm to both branch forces. The strongest equally informed comparator is an ordinary hysteresis-aware force estimator or controller (including any competent model using the same displacement history, force calibration runs, clock and actuator interface). It can use this branch information too. Thus the present audit gives **no competitive advantage, novelty claim or controller design win** for a special ASTRA operation.
+
+The physical acquisition/preparation/control bill is material: construction and mounting of the NiTi wire damper; the authors' 20-cycle wire conditioning; a displacement-driven MTS rig and force load cell; at least 512 Hz acquisition for the reported trace; repeated force-labeled calibration cycles if using either empirical lookup; and a 16-sample history buffer for the tested branch bit. The branch table doubles the number of occupied bins from 81 to 162 in the chosen scheme. The 31.25 ms lookback is a data-history span, **not** a measured latency or a demonstrated real-time controller delay. Equipment electricity, conditioning energy, control computation energy, actuator command error, load-cell uncertainty, reliability under damage, and scaling to structures or many dampers were not measured in this audit. Nothing here allows these costs to be declared negligible.
+
+A decisive next experiment would run the physical damper under preregistered, held-out earthquake-like trajectories and compare force tracking or protected-structure response using (a) the proposed branch-aware interface and (b) the best standard history-aware controller, with identical measured channels, sensor calibration, training exposure, update rate, actuator limits, latency and total energy. Randomized order and repeated specimens would separate controller benefit from drift or conditioning. The public CSV supports the input-state necessity test above; it cannot run or substitute for that intervention.
+
+## Reproduction and status boundaries
+
+Run `python3 audit.py` from this directory (standard library only). It checks the Zenodo MD5 and CSV time/schema, recomputes every crossing, work integral, lookup score and sensitivity, then writes [RESULTS.json](RESULTS.json). `python3 plot.py` regenerates the plotted cycle with matplotlib. The [original ZIP](source/Data_v1.0.0.zip), [protocol](source/Load_Protocol_v1.0.0.pdf), [record metadata](source/zenodo_record.json), executable audit and derived output are retained locally. Acquisition and arithmetic were actually executed. Material-level causal attribution, practical closed-loop control, structural benefit, full cost comparison, and novel consequential operation remain **UNKNOWN/NOT_ACHIEVED**.

+#!/usr/bin/env python3
+"""Audit measured SMA damper hysteresis in Zenodo record 17296336.
+
+Uses only the Python standard library. The source ZIP is downloaded separately
+from the URL recorded in REPORT.md; no synthetic observations enter the audit.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import argparse
+import csv
+import hashlib
+import io
+import json
+import math
+import statistics
+import zipfile
+from collections import defaultdict
+from pathlib import Path
+
+
+HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
+ZIP_NAME = "Data_v1.0.0.zip"
+ZIP_MD5 = "da06b1056528e8429e7f64e3019cb17b"
+PREFIX = "Data.v1.0.0/02_SMAWD/"
+FILES = {
+    "8w_20mm_0p5Hz": "02_8wires_sin20mm_0p5Hz.csv",
+    "8w_40mm_0p5Hz": "05_8wires_sin40mm_0p5Hz.csv",
+    "4w_20mm_pre_EQ": "07_4wires_sin20mm_0p5Hz.csv",
+    "4w_20mm_post_EQ": "09_4wires_sin20mm_0p5Hz_after_EQ.csv",
+}
+
+
+def read_trace(archive: zipfile.ZipFile, filename: str) -> dict[str, list[float]]:
+    with archive.open(PREFIX + filename) as raw:
+        rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.TextIOWrapper(raw, encoding="utf-8-sig")))
+    expected = {"Time", "Actuator1_Disp", "Actuator1_Force"}
+    if not rows or not expected.issubset(rows[0]):
+        raise ValueError(f"Missing expected columns in {filename}")
+    out = {key: [float(row[key]) for row in rows] for key in expected}
+    times = out["Time"]
+    if any(not math.isfinite(v) for col in out.values() for v in col):
+        raise ValueError(f"Nonfinite value in {filename}")
+    if any(b <= a for a, b in zip(times, times[1:])):
+        raise ValueError(f"Nonincreasing time in {filename}")
+    # Decimal timestamps in the CSV are rounded to varying precision.
+    if any(abs((b - a) - 1 / 512) > 1e-6 for a, b in zip(times, times[1:])):
+        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected sampling interval in {filename}")
+    return out
+
+
+def crossing_force(
+    times: list[float], displacements: list[float], forces: list[float],
+    start: float, end: float, target: float,
+) -> dict[str, float]:
+    """Linearly interpolate force at one crossing per branch in a full cycle."""
+    found: dict[str, list[float]] = {"rising": [], "falling": []}
+    for i in range(len(times) - 1):
+        if not (start <= times[i] and times[i + 1] < end):
+            continue
+        x0, x1 = displacements[i], displacements[i + 1]
+        if (x0 - target) * (x1 - target) >= 0:
+            continue
+        branch = "rising" if x1 > x0 else "falling"
+        weight = (target - x0) / (x1 - x0)
+        found[branch].append(forces[i] + weight * (forces[i + 1] - forces[i]))
+    if any(len(values) != 1 for values in found.values()):
+        raise ValueError(f"Expected one crossing per branch in [{start}, {end}); got {found}")
+    return {branch: values[0] for branch, values in found.items()}
+
+
+def cycle_work(times: list[float], x: list[float], force: list[float],
+               start: float, end: float) -> float:
+    indices = [i for i, t in enumerate(times) if start <= t < end]
+    return sum(
+        (force[a] + force[b]) * (x[b] - x[a]) / 2
+        for a, b in zip(indices, indices[1:])
+    )
+
+
+def characterize(trace: dict[str, list[float]]) -> dict:
+    t, x, f = (trace[key] for key in ("Time", "Actuator1_Disp", "Actuator1_Force"))
+    cycles = []
+    # The CSV has ten imposed 2 s periods in 0-20 s followed by rest. Exclude
+    # the first and last periods, which contain onset/offset transients.
+    for period_index in range(1, 9):
+        start = 2.0 * period_index
+        cross = crossing_force(t, x, f, start, start + 2.0, 10.0)
+        cycles.append({
+            "period_index_zero_based": period_index,
+            "time_s": [start, start + 2.0],
+            "force_at_10mm_rising_kN": cross["rising"],
+            "force_at_10mm_falling_kN": cross["falling"],
+            "branch_gap_kN": cross["rising"] - cross["falling"],
+            "loop_work_kN_mm_equiv_J": cycle_work(t, x, f, start, start + 2.0),
+        })
+    gaps = [row["branch_gap_kN"] for row in cycles]
+    work = [row["loop_work_kN_mm_equiv_J"] for row in cycles]
+    return {
+        "rows": len(t),
+        "sample_interval_s": 1 / 512,
+        "measured_displacement_range_mm": [min(x), max(x)],
+        "measured_force_range_kN": [min(f), max(f)],
+        "cycles": cycles,
+        "gap_mean_kN": statistics.mean(gaps),
+        "gap_min_kN": min(gaps),
+        "gap_max_kN": max(gaps),
+        "interpolated_pair_minimax_error_floor_kN": min(gaps) / 2,
+        "loop_work_mean_J": statistics.mean(work),
+    }
+
+
+def lookup_test(trace: dict[str, list[float]], width_mm: float, lag_samples: int) -> dict:
+    """Train two median lookup tables on 2-10 s; score both on 10-18 s."""
+    t, x, f = (trace[key] for key in ("Time", "Actuator1_Disp", "Actuator1_Force"))
+    static = defaultdict(list)
+    history = defaultdict(list)
+    for i, ti in enumerate(t):
+        if not 2 <= ti < 10:
+            continue
+        b = round(x[i] / width_mm)
+        branch = int(x[i] > x[i - lag_samples])
+        static[b].append(f[i])
+        history[(b, branch)].append(f[i])
+    static_model = {key: statistics.median(values) for key, values in static.items()}
+    history_model = {key: statistics.median(values) for key, values in history.items()}
+    error_static, error_history = [], []
+    missing = 0
+    for i, ti in enumerate(t):
+        if not 10 <= ti < 18:
+            continue
+        b = round(x[i] / width_mm)
+        branch = int(x[i] > x[i - lag_samples])
+        if b not in static_model or (b, branch) not in history_model:
+            missing += 1
+            continue
+        error_static.append(abs(f[i] - static_model[b]))
+        error_history.append(abs(f[i] - history_model[(b, branch)]))
+    if not error_static:
+        raise ValueError("No held-out observations covered by both models")
+    return {
+        "bin_width_mm": width_mm,
+        "causal_lookback_samples": lag_samples,
+        "causal_lookback_s": lag_samples / 512,
+        "training_rows": sum(len(v) for v in static.values()),
+        "test_rows_scored": len(error_static),
+        "test_rows_missing_either_lookup": missing,
+        "static_table_bins": len(static_model),
+        "history_table_bins": len(history_model),
+        "static_test_MAE_kN": statistics.mean(error_static),
+        "history_test_MAE_kN": statistics.mean(error_history),
+        "MAE_ratio_static_over_history": statistics.mean(error_static) / statistics.mean(error_history),
+    }
+
+
+def main() -> None:
+    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
+    parser.add_argument("--zip", type=Path, default=HERE / "source" / ZIP_NAME)
+    parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path, default=HERE / "RESULTS.json")
+    args = parser.parse_args()
+    source_bytes = args.zip.read_bytes()
+    actual_md5 = hashlib.md5(source_bytes).hexdigest()
+    if actual_md5 != ZIP_MD5:
+        raise ValueError(f"Zenodo ZIP MD5 mismatch: {actual_md5}")
+    with zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(source_bytes)) as archive:
+        traces = {key: read_trace(archive, name) for key, name in FILES.items()}
+    result = {
+        "source_record": "https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17296336",
+        "source_zip_md5_verified": actual_md5,
+        "source_zip_sha256": hashlib.sha256(source_bytes).hexdigest(),
+        "force_at_target_method": "linear interpolation between two measured samples bracketing +10 mm",
+        "interior_periods": "2-18 s, eight complete 2 s periods, excluding first and last active periods",
+        "trace_characterization": {key: characterize(trace) for key, trace in traces.items()},
+        "within_trace_prediction_8w_20mm": lookup_test(traces["8w_20mm_0p5Hz"], 0.5, 16),
+        "lookup_sensitivity_8w_20mm": [
+            lookup_test(traces["8w_20mm_0p5Hz"], width, lag)
+            for width in (0.25, 0.5, 1.0) for lag in (8, 16, 32)
+        ],
+    }
+    args.output.write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2) + "\n")
+    print(json.dumps({
+        "source_zip_md5_verified": actual_md5,
+        "8w_20mm_min_gap_kN": result["trace_characterization"]["8w_20mm_0p5Hz"]["gap_min_kN"],
+        "8w_20mm_mean_gap_kN": result["trace_characterization"]["8w_20mm_0p5Hz"]["gap_mean_kN"],
+        "lookup": result["within_trace_prediction_8w_20mm"],
+        "output": str(args.output),
+    }, indent=2))
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    main()

+#!/usr/bin/env python3
+"""Render one measured interior hysteresis cycle (requires matplotlib)."""
+
+import csv
+import io
+import zipfile
+from pathlib import Path
+
+import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
+
+
+here = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
+source = here / "source" / "Data_v1.0.0.zip"
+member = "Data.v1.0.0/02_SMAWD/02_8wires_sin20mm_0p5Hz.csv"
+with zipfile.ZipFile(source) as archive, archive.open(member) as raw:
+    rows = [r for r in csv.DictReader(io.TextIOWrapper(raw)) if 10 <= float(r["Time"]) < 12]
+x = [float(r["Actuator1_Disp"]) for r in rows]
+f = [float(r["Actuator1_Force"]) for r in rows]
+
+fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.8))
+ax.plot(x, f, color="#24466b", linewidth=1.7)
+ax.axvline(10, color="#bd561e", linewidth=1.1, linestyle="--", label="+10 mm crossing")
+ax.set(xlabel="Measured actuator displacement (mm)", ylabel="Measured actuator force (kN)",
+       title="8-wire SMA damper, 0.5 Hz, one measured cycle (10–12 s)")
+ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
+ax.legend(loc="upper left")
+fig.tight_layout()
+output = here / "hysteresis_cycle.png"
+fig.savefig(output, dpi=180)
+print(output)

Description

This dataset contains data from experimental testing of two shape memory alloy (SMA) wire based dampers, including training data from the SMA wires, sinusoidal cyclic loading tests of the dampers and real-time hybrid simulation (RTHS) testing of the dampers (see 'Load_Protocol_v1.0.0.pdf'). The experiments were carried out using the RTHS setup at the RWTHDynLab of the Chair of Structural Analysis and Dynamics (LBB) at RWTH Aachen University.

The experimental campaign was developed to investigate the performance of the designed large-scale shape memory alloy wire dampers (SMAWDs), focusing on the interaction between SMAWDs and the surrounding structure using RTHS, as well as to validate the damping efficiency and reusability of SMA-based control devices under seismic loading. Two large-scale SMAWD prototypes were tested using RTHS, with the dampers as the experimental substructure. The test structure represented both two-dimensional and three-dimensional steel frame structures subjected to multiple earthquake excitations with different spectral properties and magnitudes. The main objectives of the test campaign were:

  • Evaluation of dampers' dynamic characteristics.
  • Investigation of the influence of SMA dampers on the dynamic response of the structures.
  • Investigation of different damper configurations and their effectiveness under various loading conditions.
  • Investigation of the reusability of the dampers after strong earthquakes events.

Test procedure

The SMA wires used for the SMAWDs were manufactured by HMETech, Germany. They have a diameter of 3 mm and consist of nitinol with approximately 55.7 % nickel. The austenite finish temperature is 10 °C. No additional heat treatment was performed. All tests in this data set are performed with 800 mm wires from the same batch. Before using them in the damper, the wires are subjected to cyclic tensile loading to stabilize the hysteresis and reduce the occuring residual deformation during the RTHS. In the present study, 20 consecutive cycles to a maximum strain of 5 % with a strain rate of 0.5 %/s were carried out. For these tests, an INSTRON tensile testing machine was used. 
The INSTRON specifications are:

  • load capacity: +/- 160 kN
  • stroke: +/- 250 mm
  • working frequency range: 0 to 20 Hz
  • sampling frequency: 5 Hz.

The SMAWDs are constructed in the internal laboratory. All steel parts consist of S355 cold drawn steel. The wires are installed with achor grips and wedges manufactured by Paul Maschinenfabrik, Germany. The damper design and realized prototype is shown in ShapeMemoryAlloyWireDamper_v1.0.0.pdf. The dampers are tested with a different number of wires, different loading rates and amplitudes. Sinusoidal tests are performed with two MTS actuators.
The actuators' specifications are:

  • 201.45 MTS actuator
  • dynamic stroke: +/- 250 mm
  • load capacity: 443 kN
  • working frequency range: 1 to 50 Hz 
  • MTS 500 kN 551.23F-01 load cell included in the actuator
  • sampling frequency: 512 Hz.

Following the identification of the damper properties, RTHS tests were performed in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional structures. The surrounding structure was simulated as the numerical substructure in the finite element analysis program OpenSees while the SMAWDs were tested as the experimental substructure in the laboratory. The resulting displacements and restoring forces at the interface of numerical and experimental substructures were calculated, measured and synchronized in real-time, thus the experimental obtained force feedback of the SMAWDs was included in the next time step of the numerical simulation in OpenSees.
The RTHS specifications are:

  • simulation PC: OpenSees and OpenFresco for hybrid finite element simulation
  • real-time target PC: Matlab® and Simulink for predictor-corrector and delay-compensation algorithms
  • controller PC: actuator control
  • 2x 201.45 MTS actuator
  • 3x SCRAMNet cards (one in each PC) to minimize communication delay.

The two-dimensional structure is a steel moment resisting frame structure with three bays and three stories. The story height is 2000 mm and each bay has a width of 2400 mm. The structure is fixed with pinned supports on ground level. All columns and beams are realized as HEA 200 and IPE 160 steel profiles, respectively. The strong axis of each profile is used. In each node, an additional point mass of 1 ton is added. Two damper configurations were tested:

  • in Config. 1, only one damper with eight wires is installed in the first story middle bay of the structure.
  • in Config. 2, two dampers with four wires each are installed in the first and second story in the middle bay of the structure.

The three-dimensional structure is an extension of the two-dimensional structure with two bays of depth. The dimensions and sections correspond to the two-dimensional structure. The weak axis is in y-direction. On ground level, the structure is pinned with fixed rotation in the weak direction. One and two tons point masses are added to each node, leading to an asymmetric weight distribution. Two damper configurations were tested:

  • in Config. 1, two dampers are installed in the first story in the main (x) direction in the middle bay, one in the front and one in the back of the structure.
  • in Config. 2, one damper is installed in the first story in the x- and y-direction each.

The damper configurations are shown in 2D_Structure_v1.0.0.pdf and 3D_Structure_v1.0.0.pdf, respectively.
Three different earthquakes are applied as ground acceleration in the numerical structures: Northridge (1994), Kreta (2021) and Kobe (1995). The earthquakes are applied both in x- and y-direction. For the two-dimensional testing, only the stronger (x) direction of each earthquake is used. They are scaled to 0.15 g and 0.30 g peak ground acceleration, while maintaining the original ratio of x- and y-direction, and filtered to a passband of 1 to 20 Hz.

The total test procedure is reported in Load_Protocol_v1.0.0.pdf.

Files

  • ShapeMemoryAlloyWireDamper_v1.0.0.pdf
    • damper design and photo of realized prototype.
  • Data_v1.0.0.zip
    • contains all data files according to the load protocols.
    • the experimental data is provided as .csv files for each load protocol.
    • contains the unscaled earthquake ground accelerations used for RTHS.
  • Load_Protocol_v1.0.0.pdf
    • file listing the test procedure.
  • 2D_Structure_v1.0.0.pdf
    • illustrating the numerical two-dimensional substructure for RTHS.
  • 3D_Structure_v1.0.0.pdf
    • illustrating the numerical three-dimensional substructure for RTHS.
  • SMA_Wire_Time_Histories_v1.0.0.pdf
    • including plots of the measurement data of the tensile loading of the SMA wires.
  • SMAWD_Time_Histories_v1.0.0.pdf
    • including plots of the measurement data of the cyclic loading and RTHS testing of the SMAWDs.

File format of the datasets

The data is stored in .csv files, where each file contains the following columns:

01_SMA_Wires

  • Time: time in (s) from the start of testing (time step: 0.2 s)
  • Strain: strain in (%) of the SMA wires.
  • Stress: stress in (MPa) of the SMA wires.

These data files can easily be uploaded using the pandas library in Python. For example by:

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('Wire_01.csv')
Time = df["Time"]
Strain = df["Strain"]
Stress = df["Stress"]

02_SMAWD

  • Time: time in (s) from the start of testing
    • time step for sinusoidal loading: 1/512 s
    • time step for RTHS: 10/1024 s
  • Actuator1_Disp: displacement signal in (mm) of the first actuator / SMAWD
  • Actuator1_Force: force signal in (kN) of the first actuator / SMAWD
  • Actuator2_Disp: displacement signal in (mm) of the second actuator / SMAWD
  • Actuator2_Force: force signal in (kN) of the second actuator / SMAWD

These data files can easily be uploaded using the pandas library in Python. For example by:

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('07_4wires_sin20mm_0p5Hz.csv')
Time = df["Time"]
Actuator1_Disp = df["Actuator1_Disp"]
Actuator1_Force = df["Actuator1_Force"]
Actuator2_Disp = df["Actuator2_Disp"]
Actuator2_Force = df["Actuator2_Force"]

Important: The displacement and force signal of the second actuator is only included in test series with two SMAWDs (see LoadProtocol_v1.0.0.pdf).

03_Earthquakes

  • Time: time in (s) from the start of testing (time step: 10/1024 s)
  • Acceleration: acceleration in (g) with the original ratio of x and x excitation for each earthquake.

These data files can easily be uploaded using the pandas library in Python. For example by:

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('Northridge1994X.csv')
Time = df["Time"]
Acceleration = df["Acceleration"]
